BasePK: 3198571

Speech:
We have been doing very well. Do not worry. All you have to do is take a look at what is happening in the Toronto area.
There are an estimated 155,000 households in Canada with very serious housing problems, paying too much for substandard, crowded accommodation. An additional 438,000 are paying over 30 per cent for shelter. I am so glad the minister and I agree on these figures.
If we consider the normal expenditure ratio employed today, which is 25 per cent, that figure then balloons to 800,000 persons. However, it is revealing to note that one of the principal suggestions contained in a confidential study by the interdepartmental committee on social policy on shelter is that poor people living in public housing may soon have to pay 30 per cent. I hope that it does not make the minister uncomfortable to hear this so close to an election, but he must admit that it was a policy which was announced early last year and then quietly dropped in the summer. A lot of people have not forgotten.
The government makes a big deal out of the fact that it has met provincial requests to disentangle from overlapping administration procedures. Let me make it quite clear that it is only in those areas where principal funding has been shifted to the private sector that the federal government has withdrawn.
I hope that many of the Liberal backbenchers who live in the province of Quebec will realize how unfair this is going to be. It will not affect the Montreal or Quebec city market, but it will definitely affect the rural areas.
In a single area where the federal government retained a capital commitment under section 40, provincial governments still view this as an intrusion into their jurisdiction. Moreover, to qualify for federal contributions, loans and insurance, provincial and municipal housing agents are required to expend enormous resources to provide the mountain of information still requested by Central Mortgage and Housing.
February 23, 1979

The specific instruments for achieving disentanglement, and hence the programs, would be federal and provincial master agreements which would be prepared and signed annually with each province. To date there is anything but unanimous agreement, and only three or four provinces have actually signed.
While recognition of the value of the third-sector groups is long overdue, it is imperative that management skills and training be provided and insured through an adequately funded community resource fund program. A national urban policy must be sensitive to the fundamental social ties that bind human communities together by placing a clear new emphasis upon restoration of a sense of community through the reinforcement and preservation of communities.
Neighbourhood and voluntary non-profit groups have made impressive efforts to renew their communities in many parts of this country. Despite lack of funds and at times a lack of support from outside the community, neighbourhood-based revitalized activities have shown great signs of progress and must be encouraged.
The federal government has failed to help strengthen and expand neighbourhood and voluntary group efforts at selfhelp. It has failed to encourage cities to grant neighbourhood and non-profit voluntary groups the opportunity to participate in planning and implementing community-oriented programs. It should begin to encourage cities more actively to use the knowledge and energy of neighbourhood volunteers and the expertise of neighbourhood group leaders and staff. From all appearances, it is evident that the government is still intent on subsidizing the housing unit when it would be more useful to explore the possibility of extending federal funds, particularly as regards senior citizens, to the provinces via the global funding formula for the purpose of subsidizing incomes on the British Columbia or New Brunswick model. I was grateful to hear the minister speak of both these models which are ways that we must go in the future with other programs such as these.
One thing was made clear this week when the minister philosophized about his shelter allowance scheme. He stated that if the dollar improved, if government revenues increase, and if everything else was just ideal, he would commit his government to a housing program to alleviate the present problem. What is clear, Mr. Speaker, is that housing is not a priority of this government and that urban planning is not a priority of this government.
As stated by Mr. Hellyer, who is a former Liberal cabinet minister and a member of the federal housing task force:
If the federal government were really serious about housing costs it would move heaven and earth to assist municipalities, including the provision of cheap money for the installation of municipal services. But it proposes, instead, to concentrate on treating the symptoms rather than the disease. And that is the reason for the mushrooming bureaucracy and astronomical subsidies that have failed to do the job.
The Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program has been to a large extent one of the more innovative and successful programs administered by CMHC. The program has been applauded from all areas of the country. The government has
Housing
recognized and responded to its biggest challenges. It was formerly extended only to those areas and neighbourhoods designated within a neighbourhood improvement program area; the NIP program. So what has this government done? First of all, the minister has announced publicly in this House and in committee that the program would now be universal, open to everyone. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities were moved to extend laurels to the minister for proposed changes which would enable this program to exist on a nationwide basis. However, this respected federation and the Canadian public succumbed to one of the biggest deceptions ever perpetrated by this government. In a confidential memo between the minister and the president of CMHC it is clear that the RRAP pro [...truncated]

All right, I will read the whole thing.
There can and should be a universal program in three senses, however:
1.	any one of the over two million housing units in need of modernization aid should be able to secure a loan at reasonable interest insured under the National Housing Act;
2.	based on the criteria already in place, these units and others should be able to receive federal grant assistance-
3.	based on a phased program addressing the worst conditions first over a ten-year period, the 200,000-400,000 dwellings in need of serious upgrading and occupied by lower income people should be brought up to maintenance and occupancy standards-
Of course, that will be under our government so we will do it. I will read the last one:
What it means in the briefest terms is that while a considerable number of people can take action in the near future, because their areas and homes are in bad shape, others will need to wait for a while. It also means that rehabilitation

February 23, 1979

effort will continue to be concentrated in specified action areas as in the past, but as a matter of policy, not formal legislation.

BasePK: 3198575

Speech:
Don't you love those universal programs? In summary, then, in view of the minister's own figures that 25 per cent of the Canadian housing stock is over 20 years old and in light of his reduced-and unmentioned-budget of $56 million, I can only assume that this minister and this government live in a universe of their own. What is necessary is a long-term strategy combining housing needs, financial resorces, and the capabilities of government and industry in an effort to redress the inadequate housing policies of this government.
With respect to native people on reserves, total new construction to eliminate the present backlog and meet the next five-year needs is 23,000 units, while the total number of major renovations in the same period is 30,000 units. These requirements represent an annual construction rate of 4,500 new units compared with a recent average of approximately 2,400 units per year, and a need for approximately 6,000 major renovations per year compared with a recent rate of 1,800 units per year. During the debate my colleagues will comment much more on the great need for housing for Indians.
With all due respect to the minister, I realize he has very much on his mind while getting ready for the election. I think that is why he is in a hurry but, please, let us be realistic, and let us commit ourselves to a long-term strategy for renovation which in many ways would act as the cornerstone in any urban renewal project. We all realize it cannot be done overnight, but in committee we intend to discuss additional avenues open to the government to adopt such a strategy.
Finally, with regard to RRAP, I question why we should discriminate against the landlord when the success of this program has been that it has ensured a steady increase in the number of renovated units in some of our older neighbourhoods. More about that in the committee.
One of the remaining elements in the bill emphasizes new and expanded use of NHA mortgage insurance. In point of fact the aggregate maximum of loan insurance has been increased to $40 billion. In the committee we will want the minister to give us much more information on this clause.
AHOP has been dropped in favour of a graduated mortgage payment. The minister knows, and I know, that major lending institutions do not support this financing technique, and to gain this support the government proposes to implement a quick settlement package. In the words of one analyst, and I quote:
There are no longer any checks and balances; no rules for circumspection. The borrowers can borrow with hardly any money down. The lenders can lend with scant attention to risk. And CMHC can subsidize with magnanimous indifference.
On the one hand, we have the Minister of Finance who wants to continue to wrestle inflation to the ground and, on the

other hand, we have the Minister of State for Urban Affairs phasing in a graduated mortgage payment based on future inflationary increases in prices and incomes. The minister is putting people in an incredible bind. Under this government that is all that has been achieved. The 1971 housing dollar is worth 48.2 cents.
The cost of housing has not even been addressed in this bill. That is very serious. This week the minister announced to an audience of Toronto home builders that he was increasing the maximum NHA lending price to $70,000. Imagine, $70,000! The mayor of Toronto spoke prior to the minister that day, and he indicated that under the old price-lending structure less than 10 per cent of the families in metro Toronto had incomes which would permit them to purchase new housing. The minister has lived in a vacuum somewhere. He criticizes our leader's mortgage interest deduction proposal, but he forgets that of the 67 per cent of the Canadian people who had incomes under $18,000 in 1976, only 5 per cent could borrow $25,000. The minister and his rich! He forgets. I am very eager to see what happens to the minister when he goes out to union halls and into poor districts and talks against our mortgage interest deductibility proposal.

BasePK: 3198712

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the government still intends to introduce such a bill. However I would like to remind hon. members of two things. In the
February 26, 1979

first place, concerning complaints of citizens about administration of justice, as in the present case, the complaint would not have to be filed with the ombudsman but with the Canadian Judicial Council which, as far as I know, has considered the matter and found that there was no ground for complaint. As for the other aspect, if that lady is complaining about a municipal regulation, it is obvious that her complaint should be filed with the Quebec ombudsman rather than with a federal ombudsman who would not have the necessary authority to intervene in such decision.

BasePK: 3198738

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my question is supplementary to the one raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. Last Friday, outside the House, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs referred to a food policy which was about to be announced by the government. He said that we could expect an announcement today, although it would not come from him.
In light of the 21 per cent over-all annual rate of increase in the price of food identified by the AIB, and the justifiable concern about this matter, can the minister tell the House who in the government is responsible for food policy and when we can expect the announcement to which he referred outside the House on Friday?

BasePK: 3198785

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I rose on a question of privilege respecting language used in the House by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Loiselle). He was not in his seat at that time so I reserved my question of privilege until today.
I would point out that Hansard records that the Acting Speaker on that evening pointed out that the rules of the House did not permit me to rise on that occasion to ask the hon. member to retract his statement. While I applaud his facility in bilingualism, I wish he would use a more elevated diction. As Hansard records, and as Beauchesne points out, the language he used on that evening was definitely unparliamentary, and I would ask him to retract his statement.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the National Housing Act amendments which provide some needed additional flexibility. I am particularly pleased that the restrictions were removed from the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program so that it is no longer limited to housing in areas designated for neighbourhood improvement. When this bill is passed, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, or RRAP, as most people know it, will make available to individual home owners CMHC direct loans and subsidies based on income. Co-operative housing groups and non-profit associations will also be eligible for RRAP assistance without being limited to designated areas.
Representing as I do an urban constituency with older housing and with many skilled construction workers who could do repairs and reconstruction, I am particularly pleased to see measures that favour renovation and preservation of older housing.
Many of our Canadian housing programs up to now have been aimed at increasing the supply of new houses. For example, ceilings on the AHOP program were such that, in Toronto, buyers were limited to a condominium or a townhouse in the suburbs. But many people prefer to live near their

Housing
families and friends in the inner city without having to spend a lot of time and money travelling to and from work, hence the importance of renovating older homes and doing this in a way which makes these homes accessible to people with low incomes, whether these older homes are renovated by individual home owners or by a group of people who have decided to form a co-operative in order to provide themselves with affordable housing.
Prior to 1973 co-operative housing was treated as just another form of home ownership and received the same treatment and benefits as a single applicant for a home owner loan. I am referring here to both types of housing co-operatives, first the building co-operatives in which a group of people simply pool their resources to build their housing at the same time with each member of the group owning a unit outright, to do with as she or he pleases, and second, the continuing co-operative or the non-profit group which provide housing for members, in which case the co-operative itself owns the housing, each member has a share in the project, and none of the units in such a co-operative can be sold for a profit.
By 1973, although building co-operatives received some assistance, continuing co-operatives under group ownership had great difficulty in getting recognition and acceptance under the act. One problem was that legislation did not provide for co-operatives to obtain loans for low rental housing, except as the sponsor for a project in which residents did not have to be members. In other words, people with low and moderate income could have housing provided for them, but they could not own it through a co-operative.
Another problem prior to 1973 was that co-operatives could obtain funding only for new projects, not for existing housing, nor even for the rehabilitation of existing housing. As a result, people in a rental project could not get an NHA loan to buy it co-operatively even if the landlord wished to sell it to them. This made it difficult indeed to mount a strong national progam of co-operative housing.
Nineteen seventy-three, however, saw the beginning of some of the changes, the final development of which we see in the present bill. This was aimed at helping co-operatives to develop fully as another housing alternative, and particularly for Canadians with low and moderate incomes. The two most important provisions in the 1973 legislation were, first, that housing co-operatives could qualify for 100 per cent loans for non-profit, low rental housing; and, second, loans were made available for both the purchase and rehabilitation of existing housing. That new legislation in effect started a new form of co-operatives, one in which members are collectively owners but individually are in a leasehold position. On the one hand, they have the proprietary rights of a landlord and, on the other hand, the rights and advantages of tenants.

This agreement reflects the greater experience that has been gained in co-operative housing.
One important feature of the new legislation is that co-operative housing will be available to anyone, on a rent to income basis. Those who can afford to pay the full rent will do so. It is only by understanding what the causes are that we can hope to come up with solutions to the problems.
The cost of land in Canada for housing has been rising at astronomical rates over the past few years. One study shows that the cost of lots in any moderate-sized community from 1971 onward at least has doubled, and in some cases has moved higher in price than that. Of course there are a number of developers assembling land in urban areas. They are sitting on that land, holding on to it, and allowing the price to increase through speculation and lack of supply. One study shows just what is happening with land developers. Profits gained by large suburban land developers have added some $7,000 to $10,000 to the price of new $50,000 homes in cities such as Regina and Winnipeg. In Ontario, the Peel Housing Task Force found that profits on lots were 22 per cent of the final selling price of houses. One can only conclude that certain developers are making windfall profits, and that is a major factor in forcing up the cost of housing.
Of all the reasons I have given for the increase in the cost of housing, I think two stand out above all others, namely, the cost of land and the cost of mortgage interest rates. If we are to have any kind of meaningful government policy to deal with rising prices in housing, we must tackle those two key problems, the cost of money and the cost of land. What this bill really provides is that the trial division of what I would call the high court in the province of Ontario, the trial division in those three provinces, would be amalgamated with the district court, not necessarily by an increase in the number of judges, though there would certainly be an increase paid generally for judges' salaries. I think the objective is worth while and I commend the minister for bringing this measure forward.
I said this was important to me, to the bench and to the bar in the province of Ontario and I want to explain that statement to the minister. We have in this province two levels of courts, three if you count the small claims court and four if you count the provincial court. But with federally appointed judges there are two levels of trial courts, the High Court of Justice trial division and the county and district courts. The history and evolution of our society, increasing the monetary jurisdiction and increasing the subject matter jurisdiction of the courts, have imposed upon the county and district courts of Ontario and upon the judges of those courts a tremendous burden by way of extra workload. Therefore, I hope that through the message of this bill the attorney general of Ontario will cause
[The Chairman.]
to be reviewed once again the proposals of the report of the Law Reform Commission of Ontario issued in 1973, a really monumental work with respect to the administration of justice within the province.
A proposal was presented to that very distinguished commission by the County and District Court Judges Association. The proposal was considered by the commission. It asked for precisely the same kind of thing which is now granted by this bill to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick. In its proposal the County and District Court Judges Association laid out what a judicial system is supposed to do in society. I am reading from page 92 of the report as follows:
Modern society requires a judicial system which, without being exhaustive, possesses the following characteristics: (1) Reasonable expedition in the determination of litigants' disputes, (2) Economy for both the litigants and society, (3) Accessibility to all members of society irrespective of their means or station in life, (4) Volume-handling ability to accommodate the litigation explosion corresponding, not only with increased population, but also with increased accessibility and justiciability of new grievances, (5) Comprehensibility of the system to the public for whose needs it exists and (6) "Justice" of the decisions in the sense of confidence among all members and sectors of society in the competence of the decision-makers and quality of their decisions.
I think those are not bad criteria for anyone to consider in terms of what ought to motivate one when one is considering the construction of a judicial system. I point out that the judges were supported by the Ontario Sheriffs' and Court Registrars' Association, which is involved closely with the dispensation of justice and legal services to the citizens of the province of Ontario, in that that association advocated the union of the Supreme Court of Ontario trial division and the county and district courts of the province of Ontario into one superior court for the purposes of hearing trials, and I will deal with how that term specifically arose.
It is a matter of some misfortune and regret that while the government of Ontario adopted a large number of the administrative procedures which were laid out in that excellent, monumental and exhaustive report, for some reason which I cannot discern the government of Ontario chose not to adopt this plan with respect to the union of the courts. I do not say that in criticism. I know there was great pressure from the judges of the high court of the province of Ontario not to have this done, for reasons with which I respectfully dissent and disagree. However, it did not happen in the province of Ontario.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister reminded hon. members this afternoon, under the law Statistics Canada must have access to tax returns and the underlying principle of that requirement should be easily understandable.
In our system of government, Statistics Canada is the agency responsible for gathering and publishing statistical information on all aspects of Canadian society. The federal government, provincial governments and the private sector need reliable information on hundreds of aspects of our society.
The most important measure for a society is no doubt its income and the distribution of that income. Personal and corporate income tax forms sent to National Revenue for tax purposes are the best and most reliable source of information on incomes. If Statistics Canada were forbidden access to those returns, that agency would have to make major and costly surveys to gather the same information once again.
The general principle of the Statistics Act and even of the Income Tax Act is that an individual's business is his own business. If an individual has to provide information for tax or statistical purposes, the government must make sure that information is not made public.
On the other hand, governments and other organizations need over-all revenue information developed by the statistics system from income tax returns.
Therefore, parliament in its wisdom specifically provided that:
The chief statistician or a person so authorized by him may examine all reports, certificates, statements, documents or other records obtained for the Minister of National Revenue for the purposes of the Income Tax Act.
But since parliament also had a concern for the confidentiality of information submitted to Statistics Canada, it provided further that such information, when communicated to Statistics Canada, are subject to the same security rules as applied when they are collected.
Clearly, Statistics Canada employees must comply with the drastic confidentiality rules set under the National Revenue Act, which sets up penalties for officials or authorized persons who knowingly communicate or allow to be communicated information obtained for the purposes of the National Revenue Act.
For this reason Statistics Canada only publishes information on group revenues, without disclosing individuals' fiscal information. Those are legal provisions set forth in the National Revenue Act and the Statistics Act.

Speech:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks on clause 1 were very brief. I felt that because there were before us a series of amendments dealing with a number of points which have been presented by members of the opposition it would be more appropriate for me to address those points specifically as each of the amendments came before the committee. However, I respect the view expressed by the hon. member for St. John's East, who has invited me to address myself specifically to the difficult situation in whith home owners in Virginia Park and certain other AHOP projects in various places in Canada find themselves.
One of the amendments presented later today will be introduced by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton. Under its terms, we would enshrine in the National Housing Act a clause which would provide that, in the case of a loan made to a builder for the purpose of house construction, the builder should provide the purchaser with a warranty under a warranty program approved by the corporation.
There is no doubt in our minds that in future no loans should be insured by CMHC unless the builder offers a warranty program to the purchaser. I want to remind hon. members that I have been advocating this for a long time. As a former minister for consumer and corporation affairs I made many speeches advocating such a program, so one of the first things I did when I was appointed minister responsible for urban affairs was to discuss with the National Association for Housing and Urban Development the desirability of setting up a warranty program. We presently have a national warranty program which is administered by each provincial association. In practice, though, CMHC no longer insures loans for building projects unless such projects carry a guarantee to the purchaser. I am glad to note that the hon. member wants to enshrine this practice in the National Housing Act. I support her initiative and hope the House will approve the amendment.
In relation to the case which has been put forward in the House in recent weeks by the hon. member for St. John's East on behalf of some of his constituents who have been very badly affected by the incidents in Virginia Park, I told him in the House that the tools at our disposition were very limited but that CMHC was acknowledging the difficulties these people were facing. I assured him we were ready to put up the cash money required to enable them to carry out the necessary repairs immediately but that CMHC had no authority to make grants to these people. There is no provision allowing CMHC to do this. But we are ready to make an advance to them, to re-open their AHOP files and give them an appropriate amount of money with which to pay for these necessary repairs, and to make appropriate arrangements with the individuals concerned for reimbursement to be spread out over as long a period as possible.

March 9, 1979
Housing
Also, there were certain grants attached to the old AHOP program. I know that in Virginia Park some of the residents have an income which is sufficiently low to allow them to benefit from such grants in relation to the offer made by CMHC. I would be quite willing to re-open each individual file in order to help them. The response by the hon. member at the time was that something more had to be done and that some specific adjustments had to be made for these people.
After consultations with the representatives of these people I would be prepared to appoint someone to act as a special adviser to CMHC and to these people, to make recommendations in order to solve the problem of these residents. I recognize the difficulties which are inherent in these actions. At the risk of going beyond the legal responsibility of CMHC I think we ought to take an affirmative step which would allow these people to receive some relief, but not under the legal umbrella. I understand that they have lawyers who have put their case before the court. Perhaps through the court they will receive a much more substantial remedy than they could expect at this moment, but I am ready and willing, without prejudice to their court claim, to appoint a special mediator or ombudsman to deal specifically with their case, to re-open their file and to try to accommodate them quickly so that the problems they have at the present time can be solved.
The errors of the past ought to be corrected, and the ideal way to do that is to make sure that no loan is insured by CMHC unless the builder guarantees the purchaser that there is a warranty plan to protect him.
The second thing I want to say is that indeed, as suggested by the hon. member for St. John's West, I am ready to develop guidelines within the CMHC for dealing in the future with the builders of these projects about which there are complaints. I want to assure the hon. member that we on this side of the House are no more happy-and we are probably as disappointed and disgusted as the hon. member-than the hon. member about some of these things which have taken place in the past. Indeed, we do not approve of the conduct of builders who create companies just for the purpose of financing one project, after which those companies immediately disappear. They escape any liability or responsibility. I am ready to say to the hon. member for St. John's West that we will develop guidelines to make sure that CMHC will not in future do business with those companies which have bad records.

After any bill or other order in the name of a private member has been considered in the House or in any committee of the whole and any proceeding

thereon has been adjourned or interrupted, the said bill or order shall be placed on the order paper for the next sitting at the foot of the list under the respective heading for such bills or orders.

The paragraph is at least equivocal with respect to that matter. I think it goes much further than being equivocal. Throne we find that the government is making a commitment to better control federal government expenditures. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) introduced a new expenditure management system so that strict limits will fall upon individual ministers rather than simply on the shoulders of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens). Also we see that there will be parliamentary control in regard to the accountability of Crown corporations and that their spending habits will be scrutinized. We will have regular opportunities as parliamentarians to judge whether various government programs and agencies need to continue, or if they need to be altered at all by the implementation of sunset legislation.
It is a grand feat in itself when the federal government attempts to tackle the waste in government spending which has gone on for many years. In the area of parliamentary reform we see that the House of Commons will have its powers strengthened. Parliamentary committees will be much more effective. The average backbench member of parliament, if we can convince House leaders opposite, will have more of a role to play in discussing particular concerns of keen interest to constituents back home.
Also I wish to congratulate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). One cannot help but be impressed with the positive action he has taken in the short period of time he has been the federal Minister of Transport. In my opinion one of the better appointments is the one that the federal minister made regarding the grain co-ordinator, Dr. Horner from Barrhead, Alberta. Not only was he a well-respected politician in the House, but also he was the deputy premier of the province of Alberta. He is an individual who is greatly respected across the country and an individual who can grasp our transportation difficulties.
We have received commitments from three provinces to participate in hopper car purchases so that we can increase the capacity of grain movement. Also we have a commitment from the Minister of Transport that the facilities at the Prince Rupert terminal will be developed to a greater extent. One cannot help but admire the man for giving a commitment that within six years our grain transportation system will handle an additional 50 per cent of grain.
The national government has two basic responsibilities. We have an obligation to run the federal government competently, and to lead the nation to realistic goals. We have a national responsibility to do so honestly. If we as a national government could say to Canadians that we have dealt with the issues honestly, I think we could pride ourselves in that. That is a commitment of this government. We wish to restore faith and confidence in our institutions. The Prime Minister has taken action in this direction. One cannot help but admit that when one does not know the answers, one should be willing to admit that fact. We will make mistakes, but I am hopeful we on this side will be big enough to admit to those mistakes.
The Prime Minister has introduced conflict of interest guidelines for cabinet ministers. Already we have begun to live up to a number of campaign promises, the key one being mortgage deductibility. In the very near future we will see in

the House freedom of information legislation whereby the average Canadian citizen will have an opportunity to have a broader insight into the happenings of the federal government. It is important that Canadians have an opportunity to participate directly in the development of our national resources and, because of this, we have advocated that individual Canadians have an opportunity for direct ownership in the Petroleum Co. of Canada. It is advisable also that limits be placed on the number that one can own so that a large block is not purchased by a large multinational company, and that individual Canadians themselves are able to purchase them.
1 was delighted to see that the task force report set limits on the amount of ownership that one could have. I believe for individuals they placed it at 1 per cent, and for companies at 2 per cent.

We also tabled supplementary estimates A to those main estimates. Before the middle of November we intend to table supplementary estimates B, and it is anticipated that before the end of this fiscal year there will be a further tabling of supplementary estimates C.
The reason I mention that is that I feel it is important, as we consider the spending plans of this government, which are to some degree an extension of the plans of the former government, that we be candid with the Canadian public as to what is the reality of Canada's fiscal position at the present time. I say that because you will recall that when I was tabling, in the rather routine way that it is done, the main estimates for the current fiscal year, the House leader for the opposition party seemed to chide or somehow or other try to get me to say whether I "approve", to use his word, or recommend the main estimates to this House. 1 was very curious why the House leader for the opposition would have chosen that day to appear to be, if not naive, rather childish, knowing as he does that it is certainly not traditional for the person who simply tables the main estimates to make some statement that he recommends them or approves them.

Naturally, knowing that he is a great scholar of the English language, I thought 1 had better go to the Oxford dictionary to see what in fact is meant by the word "recommend". I think it is interesting to get that on the record. Oxford says that to recommend is to give in charge to God a person, his care, etc.; to speak or write of in favour or trial; say something is fit. When we turn to the word "approve", we find it means to confirm, sanction, commend, pronounce or consider good.
When you think of the significance of those two words as defined in the Oxford dictionary, I am a little pressed to understand why the House leader used the word "recommend". Mr. Speaker, how the whole population of Canada must be glad tonight to have elected a minority government last May 22, especially the people from the constituency of Abitibi who know very well, as they always did, that a minority government at last brings the
Old Age Security
legislation the people want. Suffice to recall the year 1972 when the party which today forms the official opposition was then a minority government and when we saw so many pieces of legislation like the one we are dealing with today!
A while ago I was listening to the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau) grumbling against the bill introduced in the House by this government. I remember that during the 30th Parliament I sat on the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, when the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) was the incumbent minister and I recall urging him a number of times to improve the Old Age Security Act. How the costs were high, then, Mr. Speaker! And yet older people now have to cope with a higher cost of living, but since we have a minority government it will be introducing measures like the one we are dealing with today precisely because it wants to give Canadians legislation with which they will be happy.
Mr. Speaker, I want therefore to commend this new government on this welcome measure. If it carries, and I have no doubt that it will, the proposal will enable people 60 to 65 who now receive the spouse's allowance to have something the Social Credit Party has been urging for years, the right to their pensions even when their spouses die. Until this legislation does pass, these people are cut off from any benefit or possible income for their survival. So, on my behalf and that of my constituents in Abitibi, I once more commend this government for bringing forward such a bill.
This is a great improvement to the current act, under which the allowance is maintained only for six months after the pensioner's death. As my colleague from Rimouski indicated earlier, we had been requesting the previous government to improve the act for the benefit of people who gave so many years of their lives, who worked hard so that this country may be a good place to live in. Unfortunately, the good must pay for the bad. And the aged were paying for the bad. All they could do was to beg for a small pension from social welfare in order to pay their rent; they no longer had any money to eat.
Mr. Speaker, it is a known fact that the aged are the most underprivileged in our society. It may be remembered that the late Real Caouette used to advocate a complete review of the Old Age Security Act. Of course, there were improvements: cost of living indexing of pensions, the supplement, and the spouse's allowance. Those measures were aimed essentially at protecting the aged against inflation, as we said earlier, but did very little generally to improve their circumstances.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, this legislation is an excellent start, and it is my wish that people over 60 can one day get the full spouse's allowance. That may have been an amendment we moved at the health, welfare and social affairs committee to recommend that a pension be paid to anyone aged 60 who wants to leave the labour force to make room for younger people who are now receiving unemployment insurance and welfare payments.

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
We hope that some day this government which represents the Canadian people, the same government which has decided against the guaranteed annual income, might bring forward another improvement to this bill so as to allow a 60 year old worker to leave the labour market.

I also took up this important theme once again during the last election campaign, and at that time I did not suspect in the least that my Progressive Conservative opponent might advocate such legislation. 1 think that my Progressive Conservative opponent in the last election must be very pleased about his government, even though we in the opposition propose the solutions that the entire population wants.

Something which perhaps the minister may not know is that the wording is in our Bill C-27, to convert the Post Office into a Crown corporation. The government has not invented anything.

Postal Rates
interested groups. In other words, we wanted to ensure that there would be a smooth start for the Crown corporation. It was also well known that part of the reason for the use of section 13 was to avoid taking up valuable time in a busy parliamentary schedule, and to give six months notice to postal users. However, rate increases were announced in the House of Commons and discussed there as well.
It was mentioned that we were bypassing Parliament. I found this curious coming from a government which has waited for so long before calling Parliament, the longest period in history without a Parliament. This in itself implies a criticism of the present administration's attitude to Parliament in relation to postal rates.

Does it mean that the government plans to delay or shelve introducing Crown corporation legislation, when it has had so much time to prepare or modify that legislation? October 22, 1979
Postal Rates

Christmas 1980? Christmas 1981? We looked for a new start, a risorgimento as the Italians say-a new beginning. We did not get it. We got the minister with other responsibilities, and the Post Office is just a side issue.

One would have thought that a new government that wanted to show good faith, that had no record and that did not have to apologize for the mistakes of the past, would have wiped out those 60,000 grievances. Negotiations for a new contract will take place soon and those grievances can only cause problems.

They may know how to run a private enterprise corporation where profit is the motive, but they have a very narrow view when running something that is service oriented, where it is important for workers to get along with management. The thrust of the Post Office is to provide service to the people who pay for it, namely, taxpayers. Adjournment Debate
bring any matter under inquiry to the attention of the Attorney General under the provisions of Section 13 or Section 15 of the Combines Investigation Act. Section 15 provides that the director may, at any stage of an inquiry, remit evidence to the Attorney General of Canada for consideration, to determine whether an offence has been or is about to be committed, and for such action as the Attorney General may be pleased to take.
In dealing with a case where a matter has been referred to him, the Attorney General is unquestionably entitled to obtain both information and advice from whatever sources he sees fit, including his colleagues in cabinet. The decision he takes in particular cases must, however, in the last analysis, be his decision. The Attorney General does not act on directions from his colleagues, other members of Parliament or anyone else, in discharging his duties in the enforcement of the law. On the other hand, he must be prepared to answer to Parliament for what he has done after he makes his final decision. These principles are well known and established, not only in Canada, but in every common law jurisdiction. I refer particularly to the United Kingdom where the practice, of course, grew up.
I should like to read into the record the best statement on the question that I am aware of, which may be found in a work prepared by Professor Edwards of the University of Toronto entitled "Law Officers of the Crown". I shall give my hon. friend the reference when I finish. Professor Edwards said:
I think the true doctrine is... that it is the duty of an Attorney General, in deciding whether or not to authorize the prosecution, to acquaint himself with all the relevant facts, including, for instance, the effect which the prosecution, successful or unsuccessful as the case may be, would have upon public morale and order, and with any other consideration affecting public policy. In order so to inform himself, he may, although I do not think he is obliged to, consult with any of his colleagues in the government, and indeed, as Lord Simon once said, he would in some cases be a fool if he did not. On the other hand, the assistance of his colleagues is confined to informing him of particular considerations which might affect his own decision, and does not consist, and must not consist, in telling him what that decision ought to be. The responsibility for the eventual decision rests with the Attorney General, and he is not to be put, and is not put, under pressure by his colleagues in the matter. dence clearly indicates that it is not serious. The second argument is much more fundamental, and that is the fairness argument. May I say, with respect, that I do not think anything we heard from the parliamentary secretary- whom 1 am glad to compliment on his fairness and patience in dealing at length with our questions over the past couple of days-addressed the question of fairness and, I suggest, it is the philosophical difference between our parties which lies at the root of this. Of course, these are legitimate arguments in our capitalist society, and it is important for the people of Canada to recognize that there is one party that is talking about fairness and that another party is talking about incentive and accumulation of wealth, and over here there is still another party which is talking about nothing.

Order, please. The point raised by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) illustrates many of the problems concerning the organization of private members' bills for private members' hour. The reason why the bills which were referred to are not printed was partly given by the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), and that is that at the outset of a session bills are submitted in time for the draw but merely contain the title, and the staff is left waiting for instructions from hon. members as to what they want in their bills. The bills cannot be printed without knowing what will be in them.
Today there are only four bills, Nos. 202, 203, 209 and 213 that are printed. I am told that the four members concerned were not ready to proceed, although I am not in a position to verify that fact. From past experience-and I must pay a compliment to those who have been left with the job of organizing the workings of this matter-members are

November 2, 1979
Order of Business
approached when their bill comes due, and, if they are ready to proceed, then the Elouse proceeds with the bill.
1 would like to take hon. members back to a similar debate which took place on November 14 and November 28, 1977, and was followed by a ruling made by myself on December 5, 1977. In that ruling I suggested to the House a procedure as to workings of our Standing Orders 18(1), 19(1) and 49(1) during private members' hour. At that time I suggested a practice which we have been following since then, and that is the practice of standing bills by unanimous consent if possible without requesting the government to stand an item of business during private members' hour. This, I think, has simplified our procedure, but at the same time it has allowed members to complain about the selection of bills.
Having said that, I would like to read to hon. members a question 1 had in my mind at the conclusion of the debate on November 28, 1977. It reads:
Is the fact that the government has been co-ordinating this recent procedure which has developed, bringing about some suspicion?
At that time I was referring to the procedure whereby the Privy Council Office organized and planned the work of the private members' business on a weekly basis. I was questioning the reason which prompted the hon. member for Vaudreuil to raise the question at that time. I went on to say:
Would there be a valid objective in suggesting that such programming of private members' business ought to come under the Deputy Speakership or the Chair in general? Should there be some kind of co-ordination by the Chair or Deputy Speaker who officiates at the drawing of the order of business for private members at the beginning of the session?
That point I think was touched by the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre). Without insinuating that this alternative would be the solution to our problem, the Chair is often found in a situation where it does not have all the elements to a problem. It could be a problem of procedure, planning, or the workings of the House. We hear members complaining that they have not been contacted by the Privy Council office when they were ready to proceed, but then perhaps they were not in their offices.
Part of the organization of private members' business is conducted in one place, while the procedural aspects are conducted around the Chair. Perhaps this is something which our committee on procedure could explore. We are at this moment discussing the matter around the Chair. I can tell hon. members that the Clerk of the House and the Deputy Speaker's office are setting up an office for private members' business which will scrutinize all bills, and it will have an appointed officer who will specifically examine all bills to be debated in this House during private members' hour. This office will be concerned with the private members' hour, and will accept complaints with regard to it. The question could be raised as to whether this office should co-ordinate all facets of the private members' hour. I do not know, and I will leave that matter to hon. members for discussion. I am prepared to listen to any hon. members who wish to act on what I have said.

I want to deal directly with the questions laid out in the motion, even though they were not all addressed by the Leader of the Official Opposition.

I would like, first, to deal with the question of oil supplies to Eastern Canada, namely Quebec and the Maritime provinces.
I believe the best way to describe the situation at this time is to say that it is tight but under control. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) as well as the chairman of the National Energy Board have been constantly monitoring the situation for weeks and months.
We did not wait until we had a crisis this winter to act, and concrete steps have been taken to deal with any major problem that could occur in coming months. That is why the volume of our exports of crude oil abroad have been reduced considerably, in fact nearly eliminated so as to fully meet the demand by Canadian refiners. With the approval of the government, the National Energy Board is allowed to swap Canadian western crude for additional supplies of foreign oil to eastern Canada. The National Energy Board recently approved swaps totalling 2.5 million barrels that will practically all go to Quebec refineries.
In addition, the National Energy Board asked Interprovincial Pipe Line to amend its regulations so as not to penalize corporations that have not done business with it in the past.

That will have a direct effect on a group of heating oil distributors in Quebec who are thus given access to 450,000 barrels of crude oil from western Canada. Other steps that would take too long to enumerate here today have also been taken to ensure as much as possible the security of oil supplies to Quebec and the maritime provinces.
However, I would like to add that if we were to face major interruptions in coming months we will not hesitate to use the powers we have under the Energy Supply Emergency Act. 1 do not believe this will be necessary but if the situation ever called for it, my government will not hesitate to act so the citizens of Quebec and the maritimes will not have to face an oil shortage this winter.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us this afternoon a non-confidence motion put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau). The motion reads as follows, and I quote:
That this House has no confidence in the government because it will cause severe economic hardship for the Canadian people this winter: first, through its neglect of the grave possibility of shortages in heating fuel; second, through its failure to support existing intergovernmental agreements on oil pricing and supply; third, through its inability to conclude agreements preventing immoderate price increases in the future; and, fourth, through its acceptance of record high interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to point out that making up one's mind on such a motion is a very difficult and delicate task. Canadians who are now listening to us must also be in this same predicament for if such a motion were to be accepted, this non-confidence motion against the new government would be tantamount to a confidence motion for the previous government.
Since coming to this House, 1 have heard hon. members from the opposition question the government. They ask the same questions the new government members were asking when they were the opposition. And I have heard government members, the new Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) for instance, give the same answers as the previous government did when

they were in power. 1 see the Prime Minister shaking his head. If he would read his statements and compare them with those made by the former prime minister, he would have to agree on this.
I paid close attention today to the speech delivered by the mover of the motion, and to the answer given by the Prime Minister, after listening of course to the remarks made by my colleague, the Leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Broad bent).
The former prime minister said the new prime minister was an irresponsible leader, that he was incapable of finding solutions to our economic and energy problems. On the other hand, the new prime minister suggested that the former prime minister, when in government, was totally incapable of solving the economic problems and bringing true solutions to any of the areas of concern to Canadians. In other words, they accused each other and Mr. Speaker, I am reluctant to use these terms, because they are hardly parliamentary, they accused each other of being incompetent, so to speak. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether both were not right to some extent. The Canadian people chose to elect a new government on May 22, and why? Because things were not working any more, and the previous government's deficits had become unacceptable. I heard the former Prime Minister suggest earlier before the House that the high cost of energy will amount to about $300 per capita, and this seems inevitable.
But he did not mention that in the last three years, budgetary deficits have put a yearly $500 debt on the back of every Canadian. The former prime minister did not mention that. And yet, it is a fact, because every year Parliament has to vote huge amounts in order to pay the interest on such a fantastic debt that long-term borrowings are now needed to make up the yearly budgetary deficits.
Mr. Speaker, how can we believe that the former prime minister, the sponsor of this motion, is sincere when he or his group does not seem any more able today than they were six months ago to settle our problems? That is why I would like to come back to the motion which is in four parts. First, it mentions the grave possibility of shortages in heating fuel. I feel this first part of the motion is extremely important. The second part deals with agreements to prevent price increases. I think, Mr. Speaker, it is far more than a ritual. I would also say that the kind of vitriolic and poisonous

words which we heard from the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), again challenging the reasons for our motion, only shows a man who is so frustrated by his own unrequited desire for power that he really should be challenged as to whose ethics are worse, and whether he is prepared to support a motion from members whose motives he does not accept. This is a serious motion-no one is treating it lightly or treating it with the kind of frivolity that hon. members opposite seem to have shown. We take the position that there is one basic fact that perhaps hon. members opposite tend to forget, that is, that they are a minority government. They neither command a majority of members in this House nor do they command a majority of votes in the country. As a minority government, they have the direct obligation and responsibility to listen to the majority. They have not been listening to the majority since this Parliament opened.
Today, we heard the Prime Minister express to the member of Parliament for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), I think, that he does not even want to listen to members of Parliament any more-he can rule by divine democracy, he can do it directly himself. But the point about minority government is that it must rest upon the confidence of the House, and the confidence of the House is held by the majority of members who are not sitting on that side. They are not Progressive Conservatives. We on this side represent far more of the population of Canada than members of the government.

The point of bringing in this non-confidence motion is very much like the old story which is told in western Canada. A farmer was seen hitting a donkey over the head with a two-by-four; he was asked why and he said, "To get its attention". We have brought in this motion to get the attention
November 6, 1979

of the government, so that it will start listening to what Canadians have to say. That is the purpose of the motion, not the cynical motives contributed by the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party nor the rituals described by the Prime Minister. We are talking about a very serious initiative. It is one instrument available to an opposition party to provide a message to the government, a message which is particularly significant for a government in a minority position. It is about time the government began remembering that fact every day; we will keep reminding it.
The reasons are clear. Since Parliament has opened we have had direct denial and contradictions of the commitments, promises, and proposals put forward by members of the Progressive Conservative Party in the election campaign. They have not been prepared to live up, by their actions, to the words they expressed at that time. It is about time their actions began to lie closer to the truth, to what they believe.
We talk about interest rates. We recognize that this is not an easy problem. We do not have a simplistic, socialistic solution like the sparrows in the corner who twitter away. There is no magic answer to the problem. There is an economic time bomb on the international monetary scene. We recognize that the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) must be careful and cautious about the rates charged. Also we realize full well that they must protect the dollar. But they have an obligation to protect Canadians as well, and to ensure that the small businessman who spoke to me in my riding on Saturday has protection. That gentleman had a line of credit of $250,000. He said, "I can last two months and then I go under because I have no protection; 1 have no satisfaction and no way of getting any assistance. The government should be listening to that kind of person.
We have been trying to say, during question period and meetings of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, that if there is a requirement to raise interest rates, there is an equal requirement to help those people who are hurt by those interest rate increases. There is an equal requirement to ask a question which I do not think has been asked: do the rates have to go as high as they have? An hon. member from Thunder Bay, gave the Minister of Finance clear documentation showing that the spread between the nominal rate and the real rate has been growing larger over the last three months, not smaller, and therefore can justify a somewhat lower interest rate. But the Minister of Finance is so busy being a down-east version of Johnny Carson that he cannot concentrate long enough to decide what economic and fiscal policies he is prepared to introduce.
We listened with great interest to the declarations of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie). In a provocative and sentimental statement the minister said, "I am concerned about the people in need." I believe that minister is concerned about the people in need, but the Minister of Finance is not because he is prepared to put $575 million into the budget this year to pay for a mortgage credit plan which has no economic use and is not going to the people in need. Is that good economics? Also I listened to the minister of housing
Severe Economic Hardship
who I think is a sincere, honest, forthright minister. On Thursday in committee he said, "Yes, there are real problems in the housing market". He indicated that people are defaulting on their mortgages, housing starts are going down, and the housing market will be in chaos.

What they failed to do in six years we cannot do in five months, but we will do it in eight or ten months. We will turn around the thinking in this country. We will turn it around so as to encourage true conservation through the substitution of other energy forms for oil, through effective home insulation programs and all of the other things that tend to provide protection and balance. We will turn this around so that this country, not by the turn of the century as the Leader of the Opposition and the former minister of energy, mines and resources would have it, is self-sufficient some time after the turn of the century-we will have self-sufficiency in this country by 1990 and we will accomplish that through conservation of our oil, through the development of additional conventional oil, through tertiary improvement and recovery of those oil resources, through the development of frontier oil both in the north and off the coast of eastern Canada, and we will do that by whatever means are necessary. Order, please. I think it might be appropriate for me to intervene very briefly here. With respect to the article in The Globe and Mail, I attempted to point out to the House early in these discussions that there was an aspect of that report in the newspaper which had to be incorrect because it seemed to me to indicate that if the President of Privy Council had made a representation, he made it as a result of the look on the faces of the Creditistes when they left the House. In fact, I pointed out to the House that the only thing which could have been interpreted, in my opinion, as any such representation by the President of Privy Council was on the day before that took place.
The second thing is that if that is to be interpreted as a representation, then I think we are setting on our course of conduct here a set of scruples which we may have to observe. However, my recollection is simply this. On that day the President of Privy Council had a suggestion to make to me, as has happened on several occasions not just by him but by other members of the House of Commons. The tone of the suggestion was very much: I have a suggestion to make for your consideration. Is it worth discussing with the other House leaders? That is as regular as clockwork in this building.
In turn, before coming into the chamber on that day and in fact recognizing one of the members of that party, I spoke with the other two House leaders and said: This has been suggested to me. What do you think of it? That was only one of several discussions which we had subsequent to that concerning what to do about this particular situation. Also I may say that I had several deputations, single, double and triple, from members of the Social Credit party who came to me to plead their case. There was nothing extraordinary about that. They indicated that they were fighting for more than simply a question or two; it was a matter of principle that they had set and so on. There was nothing irregular in any event, and I do not think any of it is a surprise to the House.
I want to set the record straight. It may have been, in the most scrupulous of standards, a mistake, as has been said, for the President of Privy Council to have done this, but I never considered it to be a representation. It was a suggestion that was made to me. The tone of it was ordinary, that I would take it up with the other two House leaders, which I did. It may very well be that that kind of conversation with one member ought never to take place. If that is the case, certainly

Mr. Speaker, on November 7 last I put a question either addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) or, as it turns out, the minister in charge of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, with respect to the home insulation program. The program has laudable objectives. The main objective, of course, is to encourage people who own private homes to insulate them and therefore reduce the amount of energy they are consuming in order to heat their homes.
Originally the program provided financial assistance to those people who owned homes erected prior to 1946. In the middle of the last federal election, on April 20, the then minister of energy, mines and resources all of a sudden came out with a new plan. He extended the program to homes built prior to 1961 and arranged for people to obtain up to $500, a real scoop, in order to assist them in their home insulation.
What concerns many of my constituents is that the standards of home insulation for houses built during the 1950s and 1960s, indeed until the early 1970s when our energy problems became apparent, were virtually the same. The same type of standard of insulation was required in my municipality and, I suspect, in most municipalities across Canada. Yet the program was extended to provide for assistance to those persons who own homes that were built prior to 1961.
There are people in my constituency who live on the same street, and some of them have houses built prior to 1961 or in 1961. In both cases the houses are virtually the same in terms of design and insulation, yet what this package does is to make fish of some people and fowl of others.
Second, there are a great number of people in subdivisions who, being good and intelligent citizens of Canada, insulated their homes prior to April of this year. Some of them have written to me complaining bitterly that they paid for their insulation with their money and now it is their taxes that are being used to help their neighbours insulate.
It is not a question of a program to assist the poor. This is not a program to assist the deprived in our society. It is a program to assist home owners, a program to assist only certain home owners who happen to own houses built prior to 1961. It is not a program that is designed to conserve fuel oil. Indeed, that is the major energy resource of which we are short. We have lots of electricity, presumably we have lots of natural gas because we are exporting more of it, and we have

lots of coal. Indeed, we have a surplus on the energy account of over $1,008 billion in trade. What we are short of is petroleum.
The program does not differentiate between electrically heated homes, oil heated homes, gas heated homes, or wood heated homes for that matter. It is a program that gives certain people for undisclosed reasons the benefit and the right of going to the treasury and saying, "Give me 500 bucks, please;" a program that says to others that they can pay the taxes to cover its cost.
I have raised the issue with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, though I must admit I have not raised it with the minister who is struck with administering the program, that is, the minister in charge of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The matter has been brought home forcefully in the committee where the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), in talking about the fiscal problems of Canada, has said that the program is costing a fortune and we do not know what the end to it will be. In looking at Supplementary Estimates (B) I see that there is another $120 million for this program in addition to the original $47,300,000 in Estimates (A). I am told, in talking with people more familiar with how to read these estimates, that buried somewhere else is another $15 million or $20 million, and the amount goes up and up. Where are we going, and why should some people get this and some people not?

The government has changed that, which is their right, but it was an irrelevant comment.
Second, it is not based on the failure to recognize that I was trying to be constructive and not be flamboyant in what is a very delicate situation. 1 got back a lot of homilies from them. My point is more narrow. That is misleading the House. 1 will grant that it may be an inadvertent action by the President of the Treasury Board. We will see in a minute.

I want to put one paragraph on the record in support of my question of privilege that there was in fact, inadvertently or otherwise, a misleading of the House. The letter, as reported, reads:
A third example. For years the labour division has been putting together estimates of labour income derived from the bureau's various surveys and other sources. At the same time, in recent years, national accounts officials have struggled with the problem of ever larger residual errors. They naturally focused on one of the national accounts' largest components, labour income, and asked for revisions which are called in the jargon "macro-economic adjustments" but more colloquially known as "cooking" or "fudging".
That is not a personnel matter or a purely administrative matter. I can see no way in which that interpretation could be placed on this letter. It goes on to say-
So that the published labour income data have been constanly yo-yoed up and down and up again the inevitable result has been that the users of these statistics, including ministers of finance, are totally confused.
Mr. Speaker, that is not merely an administrative or a personnel matter as alleged by the President of the Treasury Board when he seemed to dismiss the seriousness of the situation in his answer to me. I will accept from the hon. gentleman that, in fact, he has not read the letter, or that he has failed to understand it, but he cannot have it both ways. This is a very serious situation and one which really should be cleaned up on a non-partisan basis out of respect for the information base upon which so many economic decisions are taken in this country, not the least of which relate to the budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) will, I hope, be bringing forward in the not too distant future.

British North America Acts
whether there ought to be some limit placed upon the size of the membership. The 1974 rules were applied in the last general election and resulted in a House of 282 seats. Even at the time the rules were being adopted in 1974 there was concern that, depending on the way in which Canada's population grew, the new rules might cause a very rapid increase in the number of seats in the House, and a provision was therefore inserted into the act calling for the referral of the rules to a committee of the House in 1979 in order to permit the examination of the effects of the changes as they would be applied to the 1981 census.

This proposal to grant patents and royalties on seed hybrids raises some very critical issues and I will try to show this evening, briefly, what some of these issues are, and what perspective is appropriate to discussing them.
The first critical issue that it raises is the increasing tendency of government in this country, first under the Liberals who started us in this direction, and now under a Conservative government, to shift responsibility for important tasks from the public sector to the private sector. This is the hidden agenda of this bill both from the point of view of this government and of the last one-the desire to step up private activity in seed development so that eventually, even though it be denied at present, the government can get out of the business of research and development of seeds.

In both cases the government is leading us in the opposite direction.

A second critical issue in this regard is the power that would eventually reside in the hands of those who would have the wealth to buy up the rights to whatever new seeds are developed that would greatly benefit the farmer and the consumer through greater yields and/or decreased costs. The idea of seeds bred by a multinational corporation in order to need the pesticides or fertilizers made by the same multinational corporation, is a nightmare that cannot be written off as just a bad dream, when we look at the way in which similar things have happened over the years in other areas of concern.

Mr. Chairman, 1 think what is important at the outset is to indicate how the unemployment rate is determined for purposes of qualifying for Canada Works moneys. I think this is important not only for the hon. member but also for the previous speaker from the New Democratic Party. The criterion used is the same as that used by the previous government. It is called the labour surplus rate. It is not the unemployment insurance figure which is used in the monthly Statistics Canada bulletin.
What is done, because it is necessary to break it out by constituency-because that was the wish of hon. members and certainly the position of the previous government-is to determine the number of people on unemployment insurance by constituency. That can be determined simply through a determination of the postal code of the recipient of unemployment insurance. That number is taken as a percentage of the total labour force in a constituency as estimated by the Canada employment centres in the region. That gives us the labour surplus rate. If the figure is below 9 per cent, which this year is the trigger rate, then a constituency does not qualify. If it is above 9 per cent, then the amount of the allocation is proportionately increased depending on how high above 9 per cent the case may be.
In this case we have a situation where perhaps the labour surplus rate when determined was before a particular event took place, that is, the unfortunate lay-off of workers at IT and T Rayonier. That is the situation which, nevertheless, will have to be taken into account.
November 16, 1979

In so far as the other moneys to which the hon. member refers are concerned, those are, of course, moneys spent in the responsibility of another department.
