Oh, oh! It is quite normal for government House leaders to communicate with one another; it is always done in a democratic Parliament and especially when it is honestly done, it is a fine custom which will enable us not to do as the previous government did-introduce a bill and leave it to die on the order paper. We now have the evidence. On November 9, 1978, the Canadian government, which was then led by the Liberals, introduced Bill C-17 to promote public safety and the protection of the environment in the transportation of dangerous goods. This bill was never passed by the House even though it was discussed in February, 1979. It cannot be said that hon. members did not agree at that time because when we reread Hansard we realize that they were ready to pass that bill. Therefore, I do not know why the government did not present it once again to have it passed before the dissolution of the last session of the Thirtieth Parliament.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, a number of mishaps have occurred since then. The catastrophe in Mississauga was of such a nature as to give us abundant food for thought. Made even more aware of the situation, the government has introduced Bill C-25 which we are looking into just now; although not perfect, this bill will make it mandatory for public transporters to operate more carefully and to warn the people who manoeuvre the cars about the dangerous goods they are transporting.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, will not remedy the unfortunate events which have occurred in the past. That is clear. But it will prevent similar events in the future. To administer is to foresee. On the basis of the provisions of this bill, it is to be hoped at least that the safety of the public will be better preserved and travellers better informed about the goods being transported. Moreover, the railway workers who manoeuvre the cars will probably be more careful, in order to protect not only the people but also the property of the community.
Mr. Speaker, passing a bill is not the end of it; it then has to be enacted, the act must be made known and applied. I have always regretted and I still regret the fact that once a bill becomes law it falls into the hands of the officials who are responsible for applying it. We then come to the stage of drafting the regulations which govern the application of the act.
1 have often had to review specific cases pertaining to the implementation of an act and noted in the process that the regulations did not at all follow through on my intentions as a legislator. The rules and regulations did not follow the same train of thought as those I had hoped would apply in the application of the act. That is why I have always felt that the time has now come, when we reform our parliamentary procedure, to deal seriously with that problem, namely that once the regulations have been drafted, before they are sanctioned by order in council, they should go to a committee of the House where they could be reviewed to see whether they truly reflect
Transportation of Dangerous Goods what the legislators, hon. members, had in mind, when they are applied.
Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be wise to do so; we would thus protect not only the users and those who apply the law but also the public generally, because the act would be publicized through the media, be it radio, television or the newspapers, to ensure that the public is made aware of both its obligations and its rights. Bill C-25 would, to my mind, give us a splendid opportunity for doing so. We would then know that this bill was passed, not only for the pleasure of doing so and showing that we want to give the people some measure of protection, but also to make sure it is really efficient.
I think if that were the case we would be acting as responsible people and the law would be applied as best as humanly possible. Of course there may be mishaps along the way. Nothing is perfect. I know that, but our responsibilities as parliamentarians, as law makers, is to strive as much as possible for perfection in drafting our laws and to ask our officials, who are responsible for the application of the legislation, to do their best so as to ensure the greatest protection possible and to achieve the aims of this bill.
I wanted to take this opportunity to say that my colleagues and I support this piece of legislation and, as I have said, we want it to be well applied when it does indeed come into force.

I would like to comment on questions which have been raised in recent weeks by the defence critics of both opposition parties regarding the new fighter aircraft program.
The positions of the two parties are different, but both are ill founded for different reasons. The Liberal party now seems to take the position that the process set in place by its government should now be set aside to include Northrop's FI8L on the "short list" which currently includes the McDonnell Douglas F18A and General Dynamics' F-16. 1 am at a loss to understand the Liberal position.
Mr. Danson, as the minister of national defence, reported to this House on November 23 last year why the F18L would not be included for final consideration, and 1 quote:
-we have assessed as very considerable the risk of committing Canada to buying a sophisticated aircraft that is not in service with any other country. At this time, I consider all the various types of risks which could be involved in the development and initial introduction into operational service of this aircraft are greater than we either need or are prepared to accept.
This conclusion is shared by the present minister and has more recently been echoed by the minister of defence for Australia. The Hon. D. J. Killen reported to the Australian parliament on November 21 of this year the following:
Northrop I8L has been excluded because there is no firm program and there could be no assurance that the aircraft would be available to meet the time scales sought from our new tactical fighter. We do not believe that this aircraft, which is comparatively expensive, has advantages sufficient to continue detailed evaluations.
The Liberal party has either flip-flopped on this issue, as on so many others, or it is undertaking a stance of political opportunism at the expense of Canada's military defence. Neither does credit to the official opposition of this Parliament.
The position of the New Democratic Party is at least consistent. Its position, as expressed through questions by the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant), is that consideration of the new fighter aircraft program as an instrument of defence should be put over until Parliament has had an opportunity to undertake a review of our defence position and future requirements. The problem with this position is that it fails to appreciate two significant factors. First, over the past

decade the Soviet Union has engaged in a massive military balance. Whatever the motives of the Soviets in engaging in such a land, sea and air force build-up, the consequences are serious for the principle of balance which has tenuously preserved world peace since 1945.
Second, the previous government, through neglect or intent, allowed Canada's armed forces to degenerate so that the equipment for all three forces is antiquated to the point where Canada can contribute very little to the defence of Europe through NATO or, indeed, to the defence to North America.
These two factors, the increase in Soviet military strength and the degeneration of Canada's defence capability, were vividly revealed in the CTV interview last evening with Major-General Herbert Pitts on the W5 program. General Pitts, who formerly headed the Canadian Airborne Regiment, stated that Canada's northern defence forces are so inadequate and antiquated that as few as 1,000 Soviet troops could take over our northern installations. The NDP position simply fails to recognize these two factors. If the government were to heed its wish for a delay, the consequences could be serious for Canada.
Members of the NDP might counter my argument by saying that if Canada is so defenceless, why do we not simply concede our weakness to the United States and ask the U.S. to assume our military responsibilities both in Europe and North America? However, such a request would constitute an international declaration that Canada is no longer a sovereign nation, that we are incapable of assuming our share of responsibility for defending the free world. That is not the position which will be taken by this government.
On the contrary, this government is committed to a systematic re-equipment program which will restore gradually our once-proud armed forces to the point where Canada can assume its share of responsibility for the defence of our allies in Europe and for the territorial integrity of the northern part of this continent. Having regard for the dreadful state of our national finances which we inherited from the former government, this will not be an easy task. Nonetheless, it is one we assume as a new government, recognizing that to do otherwise would constitute a betrayal both to the members of our armed forces and to the sovereignty of this great country.
Let me conclude with a brief comment on the new fighter aircraft program itself. The program is of considerable importance to my constituency of Mississauga North because of the presence of defence production facilities. It is largely because of this constituency interest that I spent part of the past summer, along with a number of my colleagues, on a defence caucus committee. We were able to review the submissions of aircraft manufacturing companies and to weigh the consequences from both a military and industrial benefits point of view. As well I had the opportunity, while in Germany, to talk to several of our Canadian fighter pilots. This experience left no doubt in my mind that the choice for Canada is clear.

Madam Speaker, the Soviet Union's move into Afghanistan at the turn of the year caught the world by shocked surprise. The depth of international opposition can be measured by the strength of the vote in the emergency session of the United Nations General Assembly called to deal with the question in early January: one hundred and four governments cast their votes in condemnation of Soviet action. That action continues. The Soviet leaders are proceeding to tighten their hold on what was, and has been for decades, an independent neighbouring country. Such international behaviour cannot go unheeded. The country responsible cannot claim for itself immunity from the consequences of its own freely chosen course of action.
There has been broad agreement internationally that the Soviet action can only be met by concrete measures, adopted by members of the international community as expressions of concern over unacceptable and unjustifiable policies. These measures are not, and cannot be uniform: nor can they themselves secure the withdrawal of Soviet forces from Afghanistan. They do, however, reflect a full range of national reactions which when added together constitute an impressive and deliberate demonstration of world opposition to the Soviet invasion.

For its part, and after the fullest consultation with allies and friends, Canada adopted a broad spectrum of measures under the previous government which have been reaffirmed by the present government. Visits to the Soviet Union by ministers and high level officials have been cancelled. Similarly, a wide range of exchanges in education, culture, and sport, along with a wide variety of exports of manufactured goods and agricultural products, have been halted. Thus, Canadians in a broad spectrum of fields of endeavour-artists, sportsmen, farmers, academics and businessmen, to name a few-have been called upon to make sacrifices in the process of Canada's response to Soviet aggression.
In the framework of the government's reaction to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, one issue has remained undecided: participation in the 1980 Olympic Games, scheduled to be held in Moscow in July. This government believes that the international situation brought about by Soviet aggression in Afghanistan makes it wholly inappropriate to hold the Olympics in Moscow.

Since taking office, the government has maintained that it is up to the Soviet Union to create the conditions under which the games may properly take place. Obviously, such conditions do not now exist. Furthermore, there is no present intention on the part of the U.S.S.R. to create them.
We have said from the beginning that an Olympic boycott would be advisable only if effective. A few countries acting on their own, or even more countries acting in an unco-ordinated fashion, would not constitute an effective boycott. Our policy has therefore been to work actively towards an effective boycott.
In the course of the last several weeks, we have canvassed our friends in the western alliance and Third World states to determine whether a boycott of the Moscow Olympics would be an effective instrument in displaying our abhorrence of the actions of the U.S.S.R. in Afghanistan. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took a personal initiative in writing a number of world leaders on the subject. The results of these consultations, coupled with conversations I had with foreign ministers present during the recent independence celebrations in Zimbabwe, have convinced the government that the criteria for an effective boycott are now clearly present. 1 expect similar announcements in support of an effective boycott by other governments within the next days.
To ask our athletes, who have been training for four years and more for their chance at an Olympic gold medal, to forgo that chance, is a hard thing for any free country to ask of its citizens. The government is, however, convinced that withdrawal from the Olympics is the clearest and most effective way available to make plain to the leaders of the Soviet Union that the world condemns the Soviet Union's invasion of Afghanistan and its defiance of international demands for its withdrawal. If, as the Soviet Union claims, the 1980 Olympics are a vindication of Soviet policies, then by not participating in those games, we repeat to the Soviet leadership and the Soviet people that their government's actions in Afghanistan stand condemned by the world.
The Canadian Olympic Association has requested a firm indication of the government's position in this matter. The government has considered the situation thoroughly. We have decided that the circumstances leave us no choice but to urge the Canadian Olympic Association to inform the organizing committee for the 1980 Olympics that Canadian athletes will not be participating in the games. The government does not
April 22, 1980

intend to use coercion to bring about a withdrawal. It will not revoke passports or take powers to circumscribe the rights of Canadians to travel freely abroad. But should Canadian athletes participate in Moscow, they will do so without the moral or financial support of the Government of Canada.
Several nations are actively planning for athletic events in which their athletes can participate as some compensation for not having gone to Moscow. If Canadian athletes, through their accredited sport governing bodies, make it clear that they wish to participate in such events, the government will make it possible for them to do so. Moreover, the minister responsible for fitness and amateur sport will have his officials meet with national sport governing body representatives immediately to determine whatever opportunities may be available, or may be developed, to offset this setback to our amateur athletes and provide alternative competitive forums in their pursuit of excellence.
The government is aware that the final deadline for acceptance of invitations to the games is May 24. While any dramatic change in the situation in Afghanistan seems unlikely, the possibility cannot be entirely excluded. The government therefore intends to continue monitoring the situation closely. It remains up to the Soviet Union to create the conditions in which the Olympics can take place. Should it become apparent that, contrary to present evidence and, indeed, contrary even to our expectations, these conditions are being created, the government is prepared to reassess the request it is making today.
Finally, Madam Speaker, we ask Canadian athletes and Canadians generally to support this important decision which has been taken in the national interest. We all recognize the sacrifice this represents for our athletes who have trained so hard, and for whom we have so much respect.
It is, of course, not their fault, any more than it is the fault of other Canadians who are also being asked to support government policies designed to impress upon the Soviet Union that international terrorism in all of its manifestations- whether by armed students or disciplined troops-is unacceptable to Canada. The government urges Canadian athletes to respect its advice. We are confident that they, and the Canadian Olympic Committee, will have the national interest at heart and will decline to participate in the Moscow Games in the interest of Canadians and free peoples everywhere.

Madam Speaker, I would have deferred to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), but I want to say a few words in support of the position taken by my two colleagues.
There is no more fundamental right and responsibility of Parliament than control of the public purse. This very institution developed because of a concern among the people of Britain that proper control over the public purse was not being exercised. This is the central function which we, as parliamentarians, are asked to discharge as part of our responsibilities.
What the government has done by putting forward estimates that it will not stand behind, and which it disavowed any responsibility for at the very time they were tabled, has been to make a mockery of our attempts to discharge our responsibilities on behalf of our constituents. He said in the course of his remarks that there were going to be substantial changes made. He made it very clear that these estimates did not constitute the spending plan of this government. My colleagues have quoted that statement on his part.
Madam Speaker, if you take a look at Hansard pages 290 and 291 yesterday, you will find that fully one-half of the minister's remarks were designed to indicate changes that he intended to make from these estimates and to indicate why these estimates did not represent the spending intentions of the government. He concluded that section by saying, and I quote:
Madam Speaker, there are a few of the items which may have their main estimates funding level adjusted to reflect this government's policies and programs.
Clearly, the implication of that is that this is only a portion of the changes, and that what Parliament knows about today when it is asked to approve this blue book of estimates is only a portion of the changes which this government intends to make. So I ask you, Madam Speaker, how can we be called upon to discharge our responsibility to guard the public purse when the estimates which are being presented to us are patently phony, even on the basis of the testimony of the minister who introduces them?
When I tried to question the President of the Treasury Board to ask him what the spending plans of the government are-because this is central at the time we are approving the estimates; what else are the estimates for?-his response today was to refer me to the statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) two days ago. approve? What does the government intend to do with the money we approve if we go ahead on the basis of these estimates which hon. members opposite themselves say are false and do not represent their spending plans?

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege pursuant to the remarks made on April 23, 1980, as reported at pages 326, 327 and 330 of Hansard, by the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) relating to the metric program, remarks which I believe to be misleading and not representative of the truth.
The minister would have this House believe that there was full and open debate on the implementation of the metric program and, as he said:
-there were ample opportunities for hon. members to discuss this when the legislation on metric conversion was passed in this House.
The fact is that there has not been a metric conversion bill per se debate in the House. The metric program was foisted on the Canadian people through the back door in a devious manner.
The metric program had its genesis in the white paper which was tabled in the House on January 16, 1970. As is the custom with statements on motions, our spokesman, Mr. G. W. Baldwin, had only a few minutes in which to comment on the proposal. A metric converion omnibus bill was not introduced or debated in the House. Bill S-5, the Weights and Measures Act, was introduced in the Senate in October of 1970 and was
Privilege-Mr. Towers
passed in April of 1971. The bill provided that metric units could be used in trade in Canada. It would appear then that the government established a metric commission by executive order.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses stated:
-the government has no intention of imposing the metric system-
But in fact this is what has been happening in Canada. Between June, 1971, when the metric commission was established, and November, 1976 when Bill C-23 was introduced in the House, there was no opportunity for hon. members to debate the principle. A metric program was already in place when Bill C-23 came before the House. Hon. members were presented with a fait accompli. Bill C-23 was simply a catchall bill facilitating amendments to several pieces of existing legislation, such as the Wheat Board Act, the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, etc.
On page 330 of Hansard the minister is reported to have referred also to progress in metrication in the United States. To the best of my knowledge, the government and business community in the United States has not taken steps to go metric. Perhaps the minister has information we do not possess and he will be kind enough to make it available to us. At the time of the tabling of the white paper, Mr. Baldwin said:
We should think particularly of our trading relations with the United States, which of course is and has been for some years examining its position with regard to adoption of metric. Whether we like it or not, what we must do to a considerable extent is to keep pace with what is being done in the United States.
I think it might well be suicidal for us to adopt the metric system without considering what is being done in the United States.
The minister has not given the House an accurate chronology of events which led up to the introduction of metrication in Canada. I believe that my rights, along with the rights of millions of Canadians who are in opposition to metric, have been infringed upon by the misrepresentation of successive Liberal ministers, including the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Lapointe).
After studying the case, Madam Speaker, if you rule that my rights as a member of this House, along with those of many Canadians resident in a supposedly free country, have not been upheld by the actions of successive Liberal governments, I am prepared to move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That the matter of the misrepresentation of the Minister of State for Small Businesses of the proceedings of this House on metrication be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

In essence, Madam Speaker, this bill will extend the Small Businesses Loans Act for two years and, by so doing, will become part of the reaffirmation of this government's commitment to support small businesses in Canada.
As you probably know, Madam Speaker, the Small Businesses Loans Act originally came into force on January 19, 1961 to make it easier for small businesses in Canada to obtain term financing. A major feature of this program is that loans are made directly between the borrower and the lender without any prior approval of the government. The government simply guarantees a loan transaction which takes place in the private sector and in this way supports and builds on the strength of the financial community. Since 1961 the act has been subject to legislative review on a regular basis and amendments have been made over this period of time to widen the scope of operations under the act.
At present, Mr. Speaker, loans may be made for (I) the purchase of fixed or movable equipment, (2) the improvement or modernization of premises, (3) the purchase or construction of new premises, and (4) the purchase of land.
These loans are granted in accordance with standard lending procedures and are fully secured. The maximum period over which they can be repaid is ten years.

Since 1961 almost 65,000 loans have been made, to a total value of over $1 billion. These totals are a clear indication that the Small Businesses Loans Act is an important source of
financing for small businesses. The program has been growing very rapidly in recent years. In 1979 alone, over $250 million in loans was guaranteed by the government, fully one quarter of the total $1 billion lent over the entire history of the program.
The program has a broad national impact and it has steadily gained acceptance by the financial community. A breakdown by province of the total value of loans made in 1978 shows that 24 per cent were made in British Columbia, 18 per cent were made in the other western provinces, 12 per cent were made in Ontario, 39 per cent were made in Quebec and 7 per cent were made in the maritime provinces.
As for lender participation, the program was originally established to operate almost exclusively through the chartered banks and to encourage the banks to do more lending to small businesses in Canada. Since the inception of the program, however, participation by lenders has expanded. At this time, participant lenders include not only the chartered banks but also trust companies, mortgage and savings companies, credit unions and the Alberta treasury branches.
The bill before us, Mr. Speaker, proposes various changes and does two things. First of all, it amends the present act which has been in force since July 1, 1977 and is due to expire on June 30, 1980, and furthermore it amends and extends the act for an additional two-year period, from July 1, 1980 to June 30, 1982.
First, the bill amends the act so that the authorized lending ceiling which was established for the period from July 1, 1977 to June 30, 1980, is increased from $600 million to $675 million.
Mr. Speaker, when this act was last before this House it was extended for a three-year period. It was thought that a lending ceiling of $600 million would be sufficient to cover the three-year period. This amount has proved to be insufficient. With the growth of the program which I have already described, lending is rapidly approaching the $600 million ceiling. Bill C-17 proposes therefore that the ceiling for the present act be increased from $600 million to $675 million so that all of the borrowing which is required by small business will be accommodated under the terms of the present act which expires on June 30, 1980.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-17 extends the Small Businesses Loans Act for a two-year period, from July 1, 1980, to June 30, 1982.
It has been usual in the past to extend the act for a three-year period. Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
In light of the fact that in the spring of 1978 native people in Le Pas, Manitoba, were charged, prosecuted and later convicted, for hunting ducks in May of that year; that these convictions were a result of previous governments reneging on treaty agreements with native people when the government instituted the Migratory Birds Convention Act; since the Liberal government promised in 1978 and 1979 to change the legislation in order to recognize native hunting rights, and since a protocol was signed last year with the government of the United States allowing for these changes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly):
That this House instructs the Minister of the Environment to make the necessary changes in legislation immediately in order to ensure that no more native people are dragged before the courts for exercising their traditional and treaty rights.

Mr. Speaker, I asked a question of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) on April 28 concerning the ramifications of over-the-side sales of fish. I consider this to be a topic of sufficient interest and 1 would like to pursue it further this evening.
First of all I would like to say to the parliamentary secretary-I do not see the minister here tonight-that I would be the first to concede that not all over-the-side sales of fish products are bad, but it is very important, to use a phrase coined by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), in the financial sense, not to sacrifice long-term gain for short-term pain.
I would like to explore with the minister or his representative the possible ramifications of what could happen if the concept of over-the-side sales of fish is not proceeded with very carefully. Not all over-the-side sales are bad. There are many situations where the quality of fish cannot be maintained unless frozen at sea. Examples of species which fall into this category are: mackerel, silver hake, and argentine. If we, as Canadians, wish to participate in these fisheries, we will have to freeze at sea, since local plants cannot process the fish or handle the volume that can be caught. In this situation, over-the-side sales are justified. However, if over-the-side sales are used as a price fixing mechanism, which could be the case, it could lead to a disruption in the Canadian fishing industry. Let me explain.
As I understand it, there are guarantees being paid to Joint Trawlers Limited for mackerel at 12.3 cents per pound or $270 per ton, which must be one of the highest prices paid anywhere in the world for this type of product. This could ensure that Canadian processors who wish to develop the finished product and get into the world market for mackerel cannot compete. Since there is a tremendous market in Germany for smoked and canned mackerel, the Canadian industry could get into this market if it could purchase mackerel at a realistic price, having regard to general world market conditions.
Under the present policy we may have difficulty in developing our own capacity to process mackerel. However, there is a catch 22 involved here as well because, as I understand it, the federal Department of Fisheries is attempting to develop an off-shore purse seine fishery for mackerel in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. They do not want the small boat fishermen to complain about the development of this fishery. It is possible that they do not want any large factory freezer-trawlers in the gulf as they feel the offshore fishery would lead to less fish coming inshore. This is just another consideration.
Over-the-side sales to factory freezer-trawlers is a demonstration of the need-and this is one of the main points of our Canadian fishing industry. We need these vessels to get into quality markets, and once we are into these markets we can bring into the world market some of our lesser quality fish. World markets in the processing industries are beginning to stabilize after the extension of jurisdiction, and unless Canada develops a capability to participate in the high quality markets, the opportunity is not going to exist forever and we may
Adjournment Debate
have great difficulties later, which is what I meant when I spoke about sacrificing short-term gain for long-term pain.
In summary, I believe that a couple of points should be made for the purpose of debate. As I said, we should not necessarily condemn the concept of over-the-side sales. They are only justified, I believe, when the off-shore capability is not available to handle the fish and quality cannot be maintained.
I believe that such sales as a price fixing mechanism or the commensurate benefit concept, as the minister referred to it in this chamber the other day, are not necessarily the best thing for the Canadian fishing industry, and providing guarantees to foreign fishing nations or joint venture firms such as Joint Trawlers Limited could be a form of a price fixing mechanism.

It is for this reason that I open this subject tonight and invite the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, or his capable parliamentary secretary, to let us have the benefit of the justification for some of these policies that involve over-the-side sales of fish.

BasePK: 3230023

Speech:
Accidents will occur from time to time with trucks, airplanes and all manner of transport.
One of the things I regret about the focus which has been placed on the whole issue of the transportation of dangerous goods is that so much has been said about rail transport as a result of the Mississauga event. Sometimes it appears we have completely forgotten that dangerous goods are transported in planes, trucks, boats, and other modes of transportation that 1 leave to the imagination of hon. members. Therefore, it is not just rail safety which is at stake here. However, it is important to concentrate on it today because it is rail safety that is in the mind of the public as a result of the events at Mississauga and MacGregor. The best way to reduce the frequency and severity of these accidents is to reduce the amount of hazardous substances being transported. To do this, we must address the question of our dependence on non-renewable resources, which is my final concern.
We must consider the non-transportation solutions, such as reducing our dependence on non-renewable resources and changing our lifestyles accordingly. Too often we seek as a civilization, never mind just here in Canada, only technological solutions to technological problems, thus compounding our problems by refusing to see that certain technologies as such may be the root of a problem. For instance, our traditional sources of fibres and household goods, such as cotton, leather, and wood, have been replaced by synthetic goods and fibre which are extracted from and/or manufactured with the aid of non-renewable dangerous goods. This has created great conveniences in our way of life, and even greater profit for those who had the advantage of owning and marketing these new technologies and goods. But all this has happened at the expense of the environment, of those left out of work by the abandoning of labour-intensive technologies and of upcoming generations whose access to non-renewable resources for those purposes which only particular non-renewable resources can serve will be severely limited.
Consumption and disposal rather than repair and recycling has created a deficit for the future far greater in real terms than anything governments can do by way of deficit spending or borrowing, because non-renewable resources cannot be paid back. We would be far greater served as a country and as a Parliament if my colleagues on my right spent as much time whining about the deficit in non-renewable resources as they do about the deficit of the government when it comes to budget time.

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
In recent years more and more attention has come to be paid to the environment, both as it pertains to the non-human environment and as it pertains to human health. But we have a long way to go before we mature into a society that wants to know, and does know, the full effects of its way of living on human life and health, and on the rest of creation in and with which we must live. The science of toxicology, and especially of eco-toxicology, is in its embryonic stage. The fact that so very few people in the recent MacGregor spill in Manitoba seemed to know about the carcinogenic qualities of vinyl chloride, and the confusion which prevailed about the best way of dealing with it, cannot be reduced in the final analysis to the abilities or inabilities of those actually involved or to the legislation that was or was not in force at the time.
Society as a whole has been and continues to be guilty of gross negligence in the attention it pays to actual and potential harm being done to human life by dangerous products, whether it be asbestos, PCBs, methylmercury, arsenic or acid rain, or radiation, to mention a few. We must stand up and take note and consider for once that perhaps we should mend our ways and our doings, lest we find that we have sown the wind and reaped the whirlwind in the form of ecological disasters as yet unrealized but maybe only a short time away, given the often exponential evolution of ecological effects.
In the meantime, before we come to our senses about technology and a great many of the things we are up to these days, the federal government has its responsibilities, the Canadian Transport Commission has its responsibilities and the railways have their responsibilities to see to it that dangerous goods which continue to be transported are transported safely, through special measures designed to take into account the existence of these products. And that is how I see this particular bill. But we will only know how good a bill this is when we have had some time to see what the regulations are like, how they are enforced, whether the new bureaucracy that is created under the auspices of this bill has the money to enforce the new regulations, whether there is the political will to make this bill work. We will only know that as time passes.
However, it is a step in the right direction. In the meantime, as I said before, the government, the Canadian Transport Commission and the railways have a responsibility to ensure that the general context of safety, whether it pertains to rail, air, or marine transportation, is improved so that we do not have derailments and the like in the first place.

BasePK: 3230042

Speech:
The CTC must take leadership in the port of Vancouver. I will tell the hon. member who told us this. Quite a bit of research has been done. The head of the port of Vancouver, the harbours master, was the one who told me this, and it was supported by workers in several unions on the waterfront and by representatives of city council and other municipalities who have carried out major studies in this regard.
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
There is no co-ordination and no contingency plan in this area to deal with emergencies. In fact the truth is that no one is in charge. There is a morass of conflicting jurisdictions involving four levels of government, a variety of government agencies and transportation companies. We feel that the CTC must take the lead, although other jurisdictions, and particularly municipalities, are essential in developing an over-all safety plan.
From consultation with the sources which 1 mentioned in the Vancouver area-I hope the minister is aware of this-it appears that the only solution is to establish a transportation safety authority with leadership from the federal government but which will involve all jurisdictions and all methods of transportation. Such an authority would develop contingency plans to deal with the emergency, would pool the resources and divide the responsibilities of governments. It would employ inspectors, the number of whom will be increased under this bill, to enforce safety regulations. Workers should be trained, particularly workers on the waterfront. Truck routes for the transportation of hazardous materials must be studied and designated by such an authority. There must be liaison among everyone concerned with the transportation of dangerous goods.
I hope that all this will be considered by the minister and that this bill will be expanded in its application. I hope that meetings will be initiated by the federal government to develop a transportation authority, particularly in the greater Vancouver region.

We have had to journey to our mother country to change the most basic law of this nation.
1 have attempted to review the events that occurred during our attempt to change and patriate the constitution over the last 50 years. On that score there was not unanimity.

The moment we started, other people said, let us evolve a total package with a whole new constitution; let us find a process of constitutional convention, or some type of gathering, such that we can put together a whole new constitution that this nation can adopt and be sovereign in law and in fact. Some have said we should go back to the beginning and start step by step. The moment we started for the second time some province or some party said, let us evolve an over-all concept with a whole new constitution, and the process started all over again.
This has been much like a tiger chasing its own tail around and around for 50 years or longer. 1 believe we are coming back to the same process, a process in which we will again be chasing our tail in relation to the evolution of a new constitution.
A series of events has occurred in the last 50 years during which time we have seriously tried to patriate the system or find an amending formula to revise the constitution. These are the cars, as hon. members know, that are part of our modern grain delivery system. They are now essential to fulfilling the task of getting our grain to market.
The reason the minister used for not allocating any hopper cars to the railway relates back to the Crowsnest freight rate. As hon. members know, it has always been the understanding that the railways would have to haul grain from the prairies to the ports on a subsidized basis because, without that, it would be very difficult to compete in world markets. It has always been the understanding as well that, in return, the railways were granted large areas of land and other concessions. Over the years they have been granted other subsidies like branch line subsidies and so on. All of these things were never granted to the BCR.
The minister argues, and he said to me in answer to my question in the House that the subject is debatable. That is what I am doing here. He said the BCR, because all their grain goes to the west coast from the Peace River country, is not obliged to haul its grain on the same terms and conditions that the national railways haul through the Crowsnest Pass. That is quite true. However, nobody would ship any grain on the BCR if it were not shipped and transported in competition with the rates that prevail in other parts of the western prairies. The Peace River country, knowing the geography of this country, is the last part or the tail end of the prairies.
When the BCR extended its line to Fort St. John in the B.C. portion of the Peace River country, it had to compete with the Crowsnest rates. It began in 1958 to haul grain at the same price it was hauled to other ports by other railways. Therefore, that argument does not hold true. It has been very disconcerting to us because many farmers in the Peace River country have not been able to fill their quotas. There were never any cars. As well, the system is being modernized and changed to the point where these cars are essential because it is very difficult to unload the conventional cars at the ports now with all these modern elevators.

It is true, also, that British Columbia has not contributed to the extent of other provinces to the aquisi-tion of these cars. Alberta has made a commitment to purchase a thousand cars, and other provinces have purchased or leased some. On the other hand, the government of British Columbia will have told the minister during his visit out there that it has made contributions in other areas, namely, through the development of Prince Rupert, helping with the infrastructure to a large extent, and so on. So there is no excuse for the withholding of a number of these cars which are owned by the taxpayers of Canada through the Wheat Board. There is no reason a portion could not be allocated to the British Columbia Railway, and I hope tonight the parliamentary secretary will have an answer for me.

There was probably another aid program going the other way to help people in Nova Scotia. Perhaps we were sending them aid which they did not know how to use. I remember we were given cheese and apples which often arrived frozen and rotten. Somehow or other, this all seemed to make us less than human.
That is the kind of thing that will be reflected again if we let the banks continue in the direction they are headed. They will tie up poor people in poor countries by setting the same debt trap for them that my father and his neighbours were in during the 1930s.
In the coming decades we have to face not only our own internal problems but the problems of misery and poverty and the universal kind of depression in these other countries that keeps people in a depressed condition-not because they do not work but because the economic system is based on the game of monopoly. The idea of that game is to make the other person poor and keep him poor-keep him weak so that he cannot get power. In monopoly the winner ends up with all the property and power, and the loser is kicked out of the game.
After the depression a strange thing happened, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure we all remember it. In 1939 a world war broke out and suddenly there was lots of money and there were jobs all over the place. Everything boomed. But we should not think that an arms race or a war today is the way to bring our economy back to life. I think the experience of Canadians in the 1930s can be compared with the situation in some Third World countries where people are suffering today.
I think it is important when considering this bill, Mr. Speaker, that we examine how the world banking system is constructed. The frustrations of the man in the street, personal indebtedness, high interest rates and mortgage rates, that we speak of all the time in this country are the same the world over. These frustrations are experienced by all who are trying to become members of the community of nations. The banks that cause our own people to be frustrated are causing the same frustration in the Caribbean and many other areas of the world where they are a major presence. They are present in those countries for one reason only-to earn overseas profits.
Canada is integrated into the financial system of the western world. A bill such as C-6 which affects the behaviour of dominant corporate factors in the system cannot be viewed in purely domestic terms. The power and privilege enjoyed by the big banks outside Canada are related to the power and privilege they enjoy in this country.
I think it is useful for Canadians to examine how our financial institutions operate in Third World countries because that is where inflation, currency devaluation, unemployment, and foreign debt are most severe. When we examine conditions in Third World countries we can see what will happen here if we allow the same system to continue.
I have lived in countries where the devaluation of currency has reached 300 per cent per annum. Other people have probably had the same experience and know how dreadful
Bank Act
conditions are. I have lived and worked in countries where half of the population was unemployed; I have worked and lived in countries where all the money that could be earned was used to pay interest on the foreign debt.
We must ask the following questions: who controls, who decides, what are the needs, what are the greeds that continue to keep this world alive today-or dead?
Sometimes development is taken to mean that you take money and go out and build something. That is a part of development, but if we look at it in only that light we are missing the basic fact. Unless development affects the lives of individual people in individual countries in such a way that they can live without oppression or a feeling of being inferior, it cannot be called successful. One of the great problems of debt-that word that my father hated so much-is that it finally destroys the person as a person; it finally turns him into something less that a human being; it destroys. Aid given to countries that will involve them in debts just so that Canadians can make profits, is shortsighted. Increasingly, it is also because the governments of many less developed nations are desperately in search of outside capital to keep their economies afloat. That is the same thing I can relate back to the whole experience of growing up on the prairies when it was necessary somehow or other to face, as my father would find out each spring, and as many fathers had to face, how were you going to make the next year work, how were you going to get the seed grain, machinery, feed for the animals, and so on.
Those are the problems the Third World faces in another way. Each year they have to face how they are going to produce, how they are going to make their economy grow for that year. Therefore they begin the year in debt. They begin the year only with the hope that the minimum they can do is pay off the interest on the debt of the year before. They are thrown into the same ultra-hopeless position which people lived through on the prairies in the thirties.
During the last two decades, which have been called the development decades, the Third World indebtedness has risen in a most alarming way. The price of Third World exports has not kept pace in any way whatsoever with the soaring costs of imported oil and western manufacturers. This is something that western farmers like many of my colleagues sitting around me realize right now, that they are living in the same kind of cycle. Their incomes, which come from their product, grain and food, are not in any way keeping up with the cost of the machinery and the fuel they have to use. Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate in order to put before you my support for the motion that has been put forward by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis), not that we ally ourselves with the energy policy which his colleagues put forward when they were in government-I think they will understand that, in view of the position which we took with regard to their budget, and we have not changed our minds concerning that-but to respond to some of the things that have been said.
I think the energy problem poses a challenge to our economy and to our constitution. Just as we are preoccupied these weeks with the events in Quebec, I think we should also recognize the fact that there are other sources of tension in consideration which are perhaps no better exemplified than by the problem of energy. Indeed, the problem of energy also allows us to analyse our economic dependence on multinational companies and to reflect on the cost of continuing to subsidize those companies by means of pricing policies, royalty policies, and taxation policies which, if allowed to continue the way they have, would result in a transfer of tremendous funds from Canadian consumers to foreign dividend holders.
I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) is uneasy whenever we in this party talk about the multinational companies, but I would ask him to reflect upon the fact that it is two economists from the University of Alberta-who are not members of my party or indeed of any party-who have published papers over the past two years in which they point out that the problem of what the economists call the recycling of rents and revenues from our oil-pricing policies, the recycling outside Canada, poses a tremendous problem for our economy, a challenge to our constitutional ingenuity, and a challenge to our capacity to plan for the future of our economy. Let it never be said that we, on this side of the House and in this party believe that this is an easy problem to resolve. It is an extremely difficult problem to resolve, and it is with some of those difficulties, challenges and some suggestions, not of easy, quick-fix solutions but of a series of policies that, we believe, will aid Canadian economic independence, Canadian energy self-sufficiency and enable Canadians to have a greater degree of control over their own affairs, I would like to deal after the dinner hour. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this opposition day debate on energy. With the exception of the referendum in Quebec, I cannot think of an issue that is as important to the future of Canada as that of energy. When one comes to understand what the effect of the government's inaction in the field of energy may bring, it does not take too much foresight to imagine how difficult life may soon be.

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
Television has already demonstrated what life with gasoline shortages will be like by showing us the American experience. Gas stations will close on Sundays, or at the end of the month when their supplies run low. People wishing to purchase gas will have to stand in line. Unrest will grow as farmers and truckers find that they no longer have the fuel that they need in order to earn their livelihood. Consumer goods based on hydrocarbons will inflate rapidly in value as supplies of oil for industry dwindle. Finally, the government will turn to rationing in order to ensure a fair division of remaining supplies.
Eventually, public opinion will force the government to examine alternative sources of energy and new methods of introducing conservation. That was the American experience. For Canada the scenario is just one step more severe. Unlike the United States, Canada does not have areas of warm climate. When our oil runs out, people will have to deal with the Canadian winter.
Let us assume that somehow the government comes to understand the problem and manages to provide an adequate supply of oil to heat our homes, drive our cars and fuel our industries. But no matter what expense we go to in order to search for new supplies of oil and gas, eventually we will run out. No need to worry; by then we will have switched to hydrogen-powered cars and our homes will be heated by electricity, solar power or biomass.
There are only a few small details to be ironed out. The new technologies that we will need to produce these forms of energy take time and considerable sums of money to create. Canada has proved to be unwilling to invest those sums. But this is just the beginning of the technology that we will need.
It is fine to discuss replacing the energy that we get from oil, but how do we begin to replace hydrocarbons in their other functions? For example, how do we replace oil as a lubricant or as a base in paint, or for its use in producing drugs? Or how do we replace the use of oil for producing plastics and other synthetics? We have an understanding of the means of producing new forms of energy so that the average Canadian will be able to drive his car and heat his home. However, the question remains, without oil will we be able to build that car or furnish that house?
If we were to look around and try to come to an understanding of how important oil is to the maintenance of our style of life, I think that we would come to realize just how undervalued our remaining supplies are. Granted, Canada does have larger oil reserves than Saudi Arabia. The question is, will we be able to get it out of the ground when we need it? Unless the government is willing to invest in heavy oil, the tar sands, frontier exploration and new delivery systems, the answer is no. Running out of oil seems like a remote possibility until one remembers that Alberta's conventional reserves will run out in less than ten years.
Getting oil from the tar sands is a costly venture and this government, under the guise of a made-in-Canada price, has said that it is unwilling to pay that price. The Liberal party referred to the last campaign as the "18-cent election". I wonder what the people of Canada will say when they recognize the real cost of their decision. The government has committed itself to rationing in the event there is shortfall in supply. It takes great pride in telling Canadians that this is the only fair way in dealing with distribution. Through rationing, it is explained, people would receive energy on the basis of need, not according to their ability to pay, and on those terms it does seem quite attractive.

Mr. Speaker, we are now at a critical stage in the history of the maritime provinces. New Brunswick, for example, faces grave threats to its economic and social well-being and also significant opportunities to escape some of its chronic difficulties. In 1979-80 it achieved the dubious distinction of having half its provincial revenues derived from Ottawa-a landmark of dependency already passed by Prince Edward Island and soon to be reached by Nova Scotia. Moreover, rising energy costs threaten New Brunswick's single most important industry, the forestry sector, for its mills are substantially more energy-intensive than competitors elsewhere; this at a time when disease control and plant modernization are also urgent. Because social benefits reversed the net migration out of New Brunswick during the 1970s-a good thing in itself-the province has a high unemployment rate despite a respectable record of job creation.
In fact New Brunswick is just now experiencing what most other provinces began adjusting to some time ago-an increasing number of job seekers, especially women, with high educational qualifications and career aspirations to match.
There is one other major obstacle to maritime economic recovery which has been part of our condition for so long we have almost stopped treating it as a problem. If New Brunswick is to have significant manufacturing beyond the processing of its own most skilled and enterprising citizens, then it must identify and develop external markets, and it must have technologies suited to local circumstances. But large companies based outside the region have little reason to invest in such marketing or research and development, and most local companies can seldom afford it.
Those opportunities which must be seized relate mostly to energy. In terms of supply, there are several possibilities for reversing our growing and dangerous reliance on imported oil-dangerous for all of Canada because the country is already subsidizing New Brunswick alone to the tune of about $1 million a day. For Atlantic Canada as a whole, the figure is now well over $3 million.
Expanded hydroelectric capacity, including the harnassing of Fundy tidal power, is the most attractive source because such energy will never run out. We hear mutterings about the prohibitive cost of Fundy power but, as the cost of fossil fuels skyrockets and as we compare estimates for this kind of development with the projected investment in tar sands projects, we are entitled to wonder why the investigation of Fundy has been so slow.
May 8, 1980

We should also be thinking of a regional power grid and drawing on plentiful, distant sources, such as the still underdeveloped potential of the lower Churchill Falls in Labrador. New Brunswick's commitment to nuclear energy has been made in the form of Point Lepreau, which will begin to provide from 20 per cent to 30 per cent of provincial electric requirements next year. The ideal solution for pulp and paper mills is, of course, to convert wood residue to useful energy. Apart from the saving in imported oil, this would be a stimulus for new forest management techniques on both farmlands and private woodlots. Coal and thermal peat have technological obstacles to be overcome, but these resources also exist in abundance.
The question of natural gas is a distinctly two-sided one. There are enormous potential gains for New Brunswick. The Petro-Canada proposal to ship liquefied natural gas from the Arctic to an east coast port, where it would be gasified and piped to central Canadian markets, as well as the more immediate Q and M and TransCanada proposals to ship western gas eastward until Arctic resources are available-all these would command substantial activity. Q and M alone forecasts 5,500 man years over a three-year period.
The availability of natural gas opens up numerous industrial possibilities, including materials for the conversion of users to gas from other forms of energy, plastic pipe for the transmission of gas, and the production of New Brunswick's newly exploited potash resources.
The greatest opportunity of all, however, is for the expansion of Saint John's shipbuilding facilities in order to build liquid natural gas carriers. Experts are agreed that if a proposed two-phase, $50-million program to lengthen and widen the inner dry dock goes ahead, the port's permanent ice-free condition and other modern facilities will make it a strong competitor for vessel contracts.
The danger in natural gas development is long term and controllable, but only if we keep sight of it amidst the present enthusiasm. Gas is a non-renewable resource; the maritimes must learn from their mistake with oil and not become heavily dependent on another vanishing commodity. Natural gas consumption must be treated primarily as a transitional phase, with conservation and non-depleting forms of energy as the ultimate answers.
The previous government demonstrated, in the short time allowed it by the Liberals and their western surrogates, that it understood the problems and the need for immediate, comprehensive action.
Virtually every reputable economic authority in and outside the country, not to mention previous Liberal ministers of finance and energy, recognized that there could be no successful conservation campaign and no adequate development of alternate energy sources, until oil prices began rising toward realistic levels. The proposed energy bank was precisely the kind of mechanism through which research and conversion could be financed in the maritimes, and it would have provided

We should consider these statistics in the context of the bill before the House which proposes to assist people to find employment. These figures are only numbers and they really obscure the impact of young people not being able to find employment. When they arrive in the work force just out of school, feeling the challenge to get out and earn a living, and then find there are no jobs, the psychological effect is great.

It has been said many times that the employment of men and women has something to do with their dignity and feeling of self worth.

My concern is primarily for the morale and the interest of the workers of Parks Canada.

The then minister, the hon. member for London West (Mr. Buchanan), announced to the people of Canada that Parks Canada was moving out of Cornwall. The net result of that study in 1979 reaffirmed through the main estimates committee meeting in the Thirty-first Parliament that the government could save $200,000 a year by having Parks Canada in Peterborough where it would operate more effectively and efficiently. That is in the minutes of the environment committee dealing with the relocation of Parks Canada.

I remind the House that to keep this minister alive, it will cost the taxpayers of Canada $200,000 a year as they operate ineffectively and inefficiently from Cornwall. It will cost the relocation back to Cornwall of 23 families who have purchased homes in Peterborough. It will create a wasteland in downtown Peterborough where they have purchased a property and facility through an arrangement to operate Parks Canada on a five-year $800,000 lease.

Order, please. I have already explained to the House what is my policy in conducting the question period. I did say that, of course, when front benchers want to get into the question period and I know they might have a supplementary to a question asked by another member, I allow them to ask those supplementary questions because I want the question period to be as lively as possible and to bring out as much information as possible.
As for the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), his name was on the list of those who have risen in the House for several days. I do acknowledge that. I recognize hon. members in the order in which they have risen and the hon. member's name was the fifth to come up on my list, but we did not get to him before three o'clock.
Many members rise and I try to recognize them in the order in which they do so. I am assisted in that regard, to be as fair as possible, by the Clerk who tries to give me that order. 1 do my best in trying to recognize members as soon and as often as possible, but it is not possible to recognize everyone every day. On subsequent days I bring back the names on my list, but if hon. members are not in the House it is quite obvious I cannot recognize them. I cannot keep them on the list for five or six days in a row. That is my policy and the system that I have tried to establish in order to satisfy all members, but we all know that is impossible.

Mr. Speaker, in the last six weeks there has been a 4.5 percentage point decline in the
May 27, 1980

general level of interest rates. This is a relevant point to make with regard to credit cards because what we see now is a situation where the individual consumer has a great many options in the market place apart from credit card borrowing. Consumers can now borrow from banks, trust companies and credit unions at rates which are now declining at a very substantial rate and in a very significant way.
With regard to credit cards, I think that it behooves this House to say that no individual in this society has been forced to take out a credit card or to borrow on that credit card, and that there are alternatives to borrowing on that credit card which are now, with the declining interest rates, becoming very reasonable, as opposed to what they were a few months ago, particularly with regard to the cost of credit card borrowing.
Indeed, 24 per cent is a very high rate, and I agree with the hon. member that any individual who has the option should not borrow at that rate. And individuals do have that option. If one is granted a credit card, one typically has a good credit rating. We would encourage, if one is looking for funds, that one not borrow from the credit card companies, but rather through the form of a consumer loan which can be obtained at a much lower rate and which is available to anyone who qualifies for a credit card.
It is also interesting to note that individuals who have credit cards can buy goods and services with them and take up to 50 or 60 days after they have made the transaction to pay. If they pay during that period they incur no credit charge whatsoever. They have had, effectively, 50 to 60 days free use of money.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and if 1 may be permitted I will continue the debate begun a few days ago on the motion introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). With your permission, I will continue today to discuss that point and a few other matters.

Madam Speaker, in the earlier part of the motion the hon. member for Vaudreuil stated that the objective of the motion is to try to obtain more information on what is happening in the public service in the area of classification. It is to that point that I am going to address my remarks. I will attempt to respond to this request by outlining some of the more important changes Treasury Board has made to the policies and procedures governing classification in the public service.
As you may recall, Madam Speaker, the classification of 4,000 positions throughout the public service was conducted in two distinct phases. After the initial findings of the audit of the national capital area were communicated to the departments, Treasury Board continued with the audit outside the national capital area. In addition, Treasury Board undertook a pilot study of the classification system in the personnel policy branch of Treasury Board and in one operating department, as well as a detailed review of all policies and procedures related to classification in the public service.
These reviews indicated that there were significant problems in the conduct and management of, and results being realized from, the classification system as it stood. In terms of the quality of classification decisions, they indicated an unacceptable degree of overclassification; that is, putting people in a higher category than they should have been. As well, there was some underclassification and some allocation to the wrong occupational category or group. These were few and did not account for the high misclassification rate.
It was concluded that some of these problems were caused by attempts to use the classification system to solve problems in other personnel areas, such as recruitment and retention of personnel. Other problems were caused by the policies and procedures themselves.
Specifically, the classification was not-I repeat, not- designed to allow the classification of individual positions to, first of all, attract, reward, retain, sanction or remove employees. It was not designed to circumvent the intent of wage controls or bargained pay rates by reclassifying positions and individuals upwards. It was not designed to reflect perceived intergroup pay relativities. The common perception is that the pay relationships do exist between groups as well as incomes.

There was leverage, use of regulation, use of inspectors and back room deals. The government has played games with governor in council powers, with legislation, with the provinces and with Parliament. The government has seen fit to impose system international metric on the people without a sustainable reason for it.
Canadian conversion is nine to 15, maybe even 20 years ahead of the United States. The Liberal government, with its fetish for secrecy, has not even published the metric overview board's report which is a valuable overview on the whole area of public concern.
Freedom of information is a serious issue as we watch the Liberals try to centralize more and more power into the bureaucracies and its tribunals and commissions. I have always thought that limited government was a cornerstone of Liberal-Conservative political principle. That is not the case here.
As an aside, the hard-working members of the metric overview board have not yet been paid for the valuable work they have performed. That is a twist that is below the normal sense of decency and fair play expected of professional, apolitical civil servants.
I urge the government to table or publish the metric overview board report. It is a valuable document for the metric debate. All that is published is this Metric Monitor which is a biased, one-sided view of the debate. It is straight propaganda done with the people's money. In the metric overview board report you have the other side of the coin. This matter can be opened up and perhaps understood in a more equitable, fair-share way.
The democratic way would be to have a metric act fully debated in the House of Commons so that all the pieces are together in one place in one play and all concerned could make input to the process. The debate we are in today is the manipulation, by stealth, of legislation and regulation to make the standard measurement system illegal in Canada.
What has happened in Canada and Great Britain is that too much power has been gained by the bureaucracy and the academic elite. Our challenge is to strengthen the parliamentary institutions so that the skills and knowledge of the academic elite cun be used and enhanced, but with the ultimate power and control remaining with the collective expression of the people.
If we allow the government and its bureaucracy to deny the expression and will of the people due process, then we in this House have pulled the curtain down on the parliamentary process and we in Canada are dangerously close to another form of government. The insensitivity and arrogance of those responsible for metric conversion in Canada attacks the heart of our system.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to provide the House today with details of the government's assistance programs for farmers who have been hard hit by drought conditions in western Canada. My colleague, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, was supposed to be making a statement at the same time in western Canada. He has probably already made it by now as we in the House were delayed by this long point of
June 13, 1980

order which took so much time. Of course, the House is as unpredictable as the weather for the farmers.
The current dry conditions do indeed constitute a serious situation for some producers, and the government well recognizes that fact. We recognize that the producers most affected by the combined effects of a dry fall last year, a winter with little snowfall and this dry, hot spring, are the livestock producers of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Our programs address immediate problems being encountered by this group. The main problems are a lack of feed for the livestock, such as reserves of hay in the two provinces, an almost complete lack of pasture growth for grazing livestock in some areas, and some problems with water supplies.
I believe that these programs, which will be cost-shared on a 50-50 basis with the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, will solve some of these problems. The federal government's share will be $7 million.
Let me detail the programs, Madam Speaker. First of all, a cost-sharing program with the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan for feed assistance and livestock transport has been instituted. In most cases, feed will be transported to dry areas to maintain livestock. In other cases, it might be more appropriate to move livestock from these dry areas to other regions in which feed and forage is available in ample quantity. The program recognizes both of these aspects of assistance.
While the program as a whole will concentrate on these transportation and feed assistance concerns, some money will also be directed to the development of water supplies where emergency conditions have developed.
The transportation and feed assistance programs are centred in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, but part of the over-all program provides for the allocation of $1 million for similar activities in northwestern Ontario and the interior of British Columbia. Drought is also affecting these areas. Also, there will be $1 million for similar programs for the native people on Indian reserves.
Let me say that these measures have developed through the combined efforts of both federal and provincial officials. The federal task force on drought, which I ordered to be formed during the dry conditions in 1977, was instrumental in presenting me with specific recommendations on how best to handle current drought conditions. We activated this group and asked the provincial governments to participate in early May.
While livestock producers are suffering the most, cereal producers are also waiting for rain. But with some exceptions in some areas of the prairies, the cereal group could still provide reasonable yields with rain in the next short while.
So far as cereal producers are concerned, there exists already government mechanisms to assure them of their livelihood should the summer continue hot and dry. They are protected under our crop insurance plan or under the terms of the Western Grain Stabilization Act. About 80,000 farmers have purchased $1.5 billion in crop insurance protection this year. The federal government shares equally the $146 million in premium costs with participating producers. It is a 50-50
Agricultural Drought
cost-sharing program and the provinces administer these programs. The stabilization act also provides income protection should poor crop yields result in reduced cash flow. About 124,000 grain producers are enrolled in that program.
Let me say that the government views the measures 1 have just detailed as being short-term in effect. No one can provide the rain that is really needed. But federal and provincial officials are continuing carefully to monitor the entire moisture situation in western Canada, and they will be making recommendations to us as the summer progresses. We do not consider the program I have just announced as being the total program. If conditions were to change, we will have to reconsider it, and that is what I mean by saying that we will be watching the situation carefully so as to assess the needs of these people. That is as briefly as I can put it.
